title: Milestone 4 Overview
text:
Milestone 4 Student Study Guides 
 Training Improvements & Model Optimization (11 November 2026) 
 Welcome to Milestone 4 of the Industrial Surface Anomaly Segmentation project! 
 In  Milestone 1 , you inspected the physical line-scan sensor domain, Fortran-order RLE encodings, and the metric penalty on empty masks. In  Milestone 2 , you constructed your end-to-end segmentation pipeline: PyTorch datasets, industrial augmentations, combination-stratified splits, baseline U-Net models, post-processing filters, and generated your first valid Kaggle submission. 
 In  Milestone 4 , you advance from building a functional baseline to  mastering optimization, training dynamics, numerical efficiency, and scientific error diagnostics . You will learn how to stabilize training on rare defects, manage GPU memory with mixed precision, schedule learning rates, govern early stopping, and decompose validation errors to make principled engineering improvements. 
 
 1. Prerequisites from Earlier Milestones 
 Before diving into Milestone 4, ensure you are comfortable with these core foundations established in Milestones 1 and 2: 
 
 Aspect Ratio and Strip Geometry : Industrial line-scan images are  \(800 \times 128\)  pixels ( \(6.25:1\)  ratio). Native dimensions must be preserved to avoid distorting longitudinal defects. 
 Multi-Label Mask Representation : You understand that targets are 4-channel binary tensors  [4, 128, 800]  representing classes  defect_a ,  defect_b ,  defect_c , and  defect_d . 
 Combination Stratification : You understand why naive random splitting causes rare defects (like  defect_b ) to suffer extreme fold variance, and why image-level combination stratification is mandatory to prevent data leakage. 
 Baseline U-Net Mechanics : You understand the encoder contracting path, decoder expanding path, lateral skip connections, and compound BCE + Soft Dice loss functions. 
 Post-Processing Pipeline : You know how continuous logits are converted into binary masks via decision thresholds  \(\tau\) , and how connected-component analysis applies minimum area filtering ( \(A_{\min}\) ). 
 
 
 2. Curriculum Map: Milestone 4 Topics & Study Guides 
 The five core Milestone 4 curriculum requirements are organized into seven focused, progressive study guides: 
 
 
 
 Milestone 4 Curriculum Topic 
 Primary Study Guide(s) 
 Theoretical Principles 
 Practical Implementation & Diagnostic Focus 
 
 
 
 
 1. Class Imbalance 
 Guide 01: Multi-Level Class Imbalance 
 Image-level vs. class-level vs. pixel-level imbalance; data oversampling vs. loss weighting; prior shift; evaluation integrity. 
 Implement bounded square-root  WeightedRandomSampler  and class-balanced Dice; monitor rare-class recall vs. clean-image false alarms. 
 
 
 2. Learning-Rate Schedulers 
 Guide 02: LR Schedulers & Warmup 
 Optimization landscape; linear warmup stabilization; Step, Cosine Annealing, and Plateau decay; per-batch vs. per-epoch stepping. 
 Implement  LambdaLR  with warmup and cosine decay; diagnose early gradient shattering and late-stage oscillation. 
 
 
 3. Early Stopping & Checkpoints 
 Guide 03: Early Stopping & Governance 
 Monitored quantity selection; minimum delta  \(\delta_{\min}\) ; patience window; atomic checkpointing; holdout overfitting risk. 
 Build an  EarlyStopping  tracker with automatic rollback to  best.pt ; evaluate 5-fold OOF cross-validation to prevent validation drift. 
 
 
 4. Mixed Precision & GPU Memory 
 Guide 04: Mixed Precision & GPU Memory 
 IEEE-754 precision (FP32, FP16, BF16); Tensor Cores; VRAM breakdown (weights, AdamW state, activations); dynamic gradient scaling; microbatches. 
 Implement PyTorch 2.x  torch.amp.autocast  and  torch.amp.GradScaler ; configure gradient accumulation to simulate large effective batches. 
 
 
 5. Validation Dice & Overfitting 
 Guide 05: Metric Governance & Overfitting 
 The Naive Dice Trap; empty-pair convention ( \(1.0\) ); 70/20/10 official competition metric; threshold sensitivity  \(\tau\) ; learning curve archetypes. 
 Decompose validation logs into Foreground Dice, empty-pair specificity, and false-positive pixel score; diagnose learning curve failure modes. 
 
 
 6. Validation Error Analysis 
 Guide 06: Validation Error Analysis 
 The 4-view visual audit; 6 spatial error archetypes; presence recall vs. overlap recall; defect area binning (1..100 px, 101..500 px, 501+ px). 
 Build a structured error audit gallery; separate presence detection from boundary precision; formulate testable diagnostic hypotheses. 
 
 
 7. Scientific Iteration Protocol 
 Guide 07: Controlled Experimentation 
 One-Factor-At-A-Time (OFAT) rule; invariant baseline anchors; experiment audit matrix; ablation studies; distinguishing signal from noise. 
 Maintain an experiment comparison matrix; conduct systematic component ablations; eliminate harmful multi-change confounding. 
 
 
 
 
 3. Guide Overviews & Recommended Reading Order 
 Follow this recommended reading and implementation sequence: 
 
 
 Guide 01: Multi-Level Class Imbalance: Image, Class, and Pixel Mechanics :
  Deconstructs imbalance into image-level (clean material), class-level (rare  defect_b ), and pixel-level (0.2% defect canvas occupancy). Explains why aggressive oversampling shifts the model's prior and floods clean images with false alarms. Walks through a 100-strip numerical example of bounded square-root sampling and proves why validation data must remain strictly unweighted. 
 
 
 Guide 02: Learning-Rate Schedulers and Warmup Strategies :
  Explores how learning-rate dynamics dictate optimization traversal. Demonstrates why randomly initialized decoders require linear warmup to prevent gradient shattering of pretrained backbones. Compares Step Decay, Cosine Annealing, and ReduceLROnPlateau, and resolves the per-batch versus per-epoch stepping cadence trap. 
 
 
 Guide 03: Early Stopping, Checkpoint Governance, and Validation Drift :
  Investigates why validation loss minimums often diverge from peak Foreground Dice. Details the mechanics of  patience ,  min_delta , and atomic checkpoint serialization. Warns against the hazard of holdout overfitting (validation drift) caused by repeated tuning against the same validation fold. 
 
 
 Guide 04: Mixed Precision (AMP) and GPU Memory Optimization :
  Provides a forensic breakdown of GPU VRAM (weights, gradients, AdamW moments, and activation tensors). Explains how PyTorch 2.x  torch.amp  leverages Tensor Cores in FP16/BF16, details dynamic gradient scaling ( GradScaler ) to prevent gradient underflow, and demonstrates gradient accumulation to decouple hardware microbatch sizes from effective optimization batches. 
 
 
 Guide 05: Metric Governance: Validation Dice, Empty Pairs, and Overfitting :
  Exposes the "Naive Dice Trap"—proving how a lazy model that predicts all zeros achieves an 85% naive Dice score. Dissects the 2×2 contingency matrix of image-class pairs and explains the official 70/20/10 competition score. Categorizes six learning curve archetypes to diagnose overfitting, underfitting, and probability drift. 
 
 
 Guide 06: Validation Error Analysis and Spatial Defect Diagnostics :
  Establishes a 4-view visual audit workflow and defines the six spatial error archetypes (missed thin defects, false alarms on clean material, class confusion, speckle noise, boundary dilation, and fragmented cracks). Introduces defect size binning and stratified sampling to prevent the cherry-picking trap. 
 
 
 Guide 07: Controlled Experimentation and Scientific Iteration :
  Synthesizes optimization into the scientific method. Enforces the One-Factor-At-A-Time (OFAT) rule, details invariant baseline anchors, structures an experiment audit matrix, and explains how ablation studies identify dead code in your pipeline. 
 
 
 
 4. Standalone Code Examples & Synthetic Walkthrough 
 To support hands-on learning without disclosing confidential competition benchmarks, this curriculum includes complete, self-contained educational resources built entirely on  synthetic data : 
 1. Interactive Walkthrough Notebook 
 
 Jupyter Notebook :  notebooks/synthetic_optimization_walkthrough.ipynb 
 Paired Python Script :  notebooks/synthetic_optimization_walkthrough.py 
 Setup Guide :  notebooks/README.md 
 
 This walkthrough runs on CPU in under 3 seconds and interactively demonstrates bounded sampling, warmup/cosine scheduling, early stopping, PyTorch 2.x AMP accumulation, multi-metric decomposition, and spatial error binning. 
 2. Standalone Diagnostic Scripts 
 
 
 Imbalance & Bounded Sampler :  examples/toy_imbalance_sampler.py 
  Simulates a 200-strip imbalanced dataset, compares natural uniform draws against bounded weighted draws, and audits class exposure over 10 epochs. 
 
 
 Learning Rate Scheduler Simulator :  examples/toy_scheduler_visualizer.py 
  Simulates and tabulates learning-rate trajectories across Warmup + Cosine, StepLR, and ReduceLROnPlateau. 
 
 
 Early Stopping & Checkpoint Rollback :  examples/toy_early_stopping.py 
  Executes an early stopping tracker across 20 validation epochs, demonstrating patience counting, noise filtering ( min_delta ), and automatic weight restoration. 
 
 
 PyTorch 2.x AMP Lifecycle :  examples/toy_amp_lifecycle.py 
  Demonstrates  torch.amp.autocast ,  torch.amp.GradScaler , microbatch accumulation, unscaling, and gradient norm clipping on toy tensors. 
 
 
 Validation Error Analyzer :  examples/toy_error_analyzer.py 
  Decomposes validation predictions into presence recall, overlap recall, clean-image specificity, conditional Dice, and defect size bins. 
 
 
 
 5. Teaching Philosophy and Boundaries 
 These study guides are designed as a  scientific guide, not a hyperparameter cheat sheet : 
 
 They explain the underlying mathematics, numerical mechanics, failure modes, and debugging protocols. 
 They do  not  provide pre-computed hyperparameter values, optimal batch sizes, private class weights, or pre-trained checkpoints. 
 They do  not  reveal internal exploratory data analysis findings or competition benchmarks from the private training set. 
 There are  no assessment questions or graded tasks  in this folder; all exercises are clearly marked ungraded activities. 
 You must formulate your own hypotheses, conduct your own controlled experiments, and audit your models against  data/public/ .

title: Guide 01 · Multi-Level Class Imbalance
text:
Multi-Level Class Imbalance: Image, Class, and Pixel Mechanics 
 In standard deep learning classification tasks, class imbalance is typically treated as a single, one-dimensional problem: some categories have fewer training examples than others. In industrial surface defect segmentation, however, class imbalance manifests across  three distinct physical and statistical levels simultaneously . 
 An intervention designed to solve imbalance at one level can easily destabilize training or cause catastrophic error spikes at another level. This guide dissects the three tiers of imbalance, examines data-level and loss-level interventions, walks through a concrete numerical demonstration, and establishes strict validation safeguards to ensure your model detects rare anomalies without flooding clean material with false alarms. 
 
 1. Observable Problem: The Rare-Class Silence and False-Alarm Flood 
 Consider two failure modes commonly observed in industrial segmentation runs: 
 Failure Mode 1: The "Silent Predictor"
Training Loss: 0.12 (descends smoothly)
Pixel Accuracy: 98.4%
Validation Dice (defect_c): 0.65
Validation Dice (defect_b): 0.00 (Zero predicted pixels across all validation images!)

Failure Mode 2: The "False-Alarm Flood"
Student applies 50x oversampling to rare defect_b images.
Validation Dice (defect_b positives): 0.48 (Rare defects are finally detected!)
Clean-Image Specificity: Drops from 99.1% to 64.3% (Clean images receive hundreds of false alarms!)
Leaderboard Score: Plummets dramatically due to false positive penalties. 
 Why does this happen? In Failure Mode 1, the model learned that predicting all zeros for rare defects incurs negligible loss penalty, achieving near-perfect pixel accuracy. In Failure Mode 2, the student attempted to fix the problem by flooding training with rare-defect strips; the model adapted to this artificial prior, concluded that defects are ubiquitous, and began hallucinating defects on normal, defect-free material. 
 To solve this, we must deconstruct imbalance into its three constitutive levels. 
 
 2. The Three Levels of Imbalance 
 
 Figure 1.1: Industrial surface segmentation exhibits three concurrent tiers of imbalance: image-level (clean vs. defective material), class-level (common vs. rare defect geometries), and pixel-level (defect area vs. canvas area). 
 Level 1: Image-Level Imbalance (Clean vs. Defective Strips) 
 In a healthy industrial manufacturing line, high-grade steel strips are overwhelmingly  defect-free . In our dataset domain, approximately half of all captured image strips contain no defects whatsoever. 
 
 The Physical Meaning : Clean images represent the true operational baseline of the optical line-scan cameras. They contain normal surface textures, grain boundaries, roller marks, and lighting variations. 
 The Modeling Danger : If you filter out clean images during training to "concentrate on defects," your model never learns what normal background looks like. When evaluated on real production strips, it will flag every benign surface texture as a defect. 
 
 Level 2: Class-Level Imbalance (Frequent vs. Rare Defect Classes) 
 Defect types do not occur with equal frequency. In an industrial rolling mill: 
 
 Some defects (like surface inclusions or scaling, e.g.,  defect_c ) are continuous metallurgical phenomena and appear frequently. 
 Other defects (like micro-cracks or longitudinal seam defects, e.g.,  defect_b ) occur only during catastrophic tool wear or rare cooling anomalies. 
 The Modeling Danger : In a typical mini-batch of 8 images, a rare class like  defect_b  may not appear once across 50 consecutive gradient updates. The optimizer's moving momentum buffers (like those in AdamW) decay toward zero for rare-class parameters, starving them of gradient signal. 
 
 Level 3: Pixel-Level Imbalance (Defect Canvas Occupancy) 
 Even when an image contains an active defect, the anomaly occupies only a tiny fraction of the strip.
On an industrial line-scan canvas of  \(128 \times 800 = 102,400\text{ pixels}\) : 
 
 A hairline scratch might be 2 pixels wide and 100 pixels long ( \(200\text{ pixels}\) ). 
 That scratch occupies only  \(200 / 102,400 \approx 0.19\%\)  of the image! 
 The background class commands  \(99.81\%\)  of all supervised pixels. 
 The Modeling Danger : In standard Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE), gradient contributions from the  \(102,200\)  background pixels easily drown out the gradients from the  \(200\)  defect pixels. 
 
 
 3. Intervention Strategies: Data-Level vs. Loss-Level 
 To balance optimization gradients, practitioners employ interventions either at the  data pipeline level  (modifying what the model sees) or at the  loss function level  (modifying how the model is penalized). 
 
 Figure 1.2: Comparison of data-level oversampling versus loss-level weighting. Oversampling shifts the empirical prior distribution, increasing false alarms on clean validation strips. Loss weighting preserves the natural data distribution while scaling gradient updates. 
 Strategy A: Data-Level Sampling 
 Data-level interventions adjust the probability  \(P(\text{draw } i)\)  of selecting image  \(i\)  during mini-batch construction: 
 
 Natural Uniform Sampling : Every image in the training partition has equal probability  \(P(i) = 1/N\) . Mini-batches reflect the real empirical distribution. 
 Weighted Random Sampling ( WeightedRandomSampler ) : Assigns an explicit sampling weight  \(w_i \ge 1.0\)  to image  \(i\) . If image  \(i\)  contains rare  defect_b , setting  \(w_i > 1.0\)  increases its frequency of inclusion in batches. 
 
 Mathematical Formulation of Bounded Inverse-Frequency Weighting: 
 For training set  \(S\)  with  \(N\)  images, let  \(r_c\)  denote the empirical positive image prevalence of class  \(c \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\) : 
 \[r_c = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{I}(c \in \text{image } i)\] 
 To prevent catastrophic oversampling, compute  bounded square-root inverse weights : 
 \[w_{\text{class}}(c) = \min\left(w_{\max}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{\max(r_c, \epsilon)}}\right)\] 
 where  \(w_{\max} = 4.0\)  is a safety ceiling and  \(\epsilon = 1/N\) . 
 For an image  \(i\)  containing active defect set  \(\mathcal{C}_i \subseteq \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\) : 
 \[w_i = \begin{cases} 
1.0 & \text{if } \mathcal{C}_i = \emptyset \text{ (clean image)} \\
\max_{c \in \mathcal{C}_i} w_{\text{class}}(c) & \text{if } \mathcal{C}_i \neq \emptyset 
\end{cases}\] 
 
 [!IMPORTANT]
 Why take the maximum rather than the product? 
If an image contains both frequent  defect_c  and rare  defect_b , multiplying their weights would over-weight multi-defect images disproportionately. Taking the maximum ensures that an image is sampled according to its rarest constituent defect without artificial multiplication. 
 
 Strategy B: Loss-Level Weighting 
 Instead of altering how often images are sampled, loss-level weighting scales the gradient contribution of rare pixels directly in the objective function. 
 1. Positive Weighting in Binary Cross-Entropy ( pos_weight ) 
 For continuous logit  \(z \in \mathbb{R}\)  and binary label  \(y \in \{0, 1\}\) : 
 \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}}(z, y) = - \left[ \gamma \cdot y \log(\sigma(z)) + (1 - y) \log(1 - \sigma(z)) \right]\] 
 where  \(\gamma > 1.0\)  is the positive class weight ( pos_weight ). 
 If a defect occupies  \(1\%\)  of the canvas and background occupies  \(99\%\) , setting  \(\gamma = 10.0\)  scales the gradient contribution of true defect pixels by  \(10\times\) , preventing background pixels from dominating the backward pass. 
 2. Class-Balanced Soft Dice Loss 
 In standard positive-pair Dice loss, all positive defect channels are summed uniformly: 
 \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}} = 1 - \frac{2 \sum_{k \in \mathcal{P}} \sum_{i} P_{k, i} Y_{k, i} + \epsilon}{\sum_{k \in \mathcal{P}} \sum_{i} (P_{k, i} + Y_{k, i}) + \epsilon}\] 
 where  \(\mathcal{P}\)  is the set of positive image-class pairs. 
 In  class-balanced Dice reduction , the loss calculates soft Dice independently per active defect class, and then averages across present classes: 
 \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{CB-Dice}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{\text{batch}}|} \sum_{c \in \mathcal{C}_{\text{batch}}} \left( 1 - \text{Dice}_c \right)\] 
 Under this formulation, a batch containing 7 images of  defect_c  and 1 image of rare  defect_b  gives equal loss weight to both classes ( \(\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_c + \frac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_b\) ), preventing the abundant class from drowning out the rare class. 
 
 4. Worked Numerical Demonstration: A Fictional 100-Strip Pool 
 To understand how oversampling shifts the training distribution, trace a fictional pool of  \(N = 100\)  steel strips:

 Let us calculate the total sum of sampling weights across all 100 strips: 
 \[W_{\text{total}} = (50 \times 1.0) + (12 \times 2.89) + (3 \times 4.0) + (35 \times 1.69) = 50 + 34.68 + 12.0 + 59.15 = 155.83\] 
 Now compare the probability of drawing each subgroup in any mini-batch: 
 
 
 Clean Material Encounter Rate : 
 \[\text{Natural} = \frac{50}{100} = 50.0\% \quad \longrightarrow \quad \text{Weighted} = \frac{50 \times 1.0}{155.83} = 32.1\%\] 
 
 
 Rare Defect B Encounter Rate : 
 \[\text{Natural} = \frac{3}{100} = 3.0\% \quad \longrightarrow \quad \text{Weighted} = \frac{3 \times 4.0}{155.83} = 7.7\% \quad (+157\% \text{ relative exposure})\] 
 
 
 Notice what occurred: 
 
 Rare  defect_b  strips are now encountered  \(2.57\times\)  more frequently  per training epoch. 
 Clean images still constitute  \(32.1\%\)  of all draws—substantial enough to maintain strong background representation. 
 If the student had used raw inverse frequency ( \(w_B = 33.3\) ), the 3 rare images would constitute over  \(30\%\)  of all training batches, causing severe memorization of those 3 specific strip textures! 
 
 
 5. Diagnostic Symptoms: Causes and Checks 
 
 
 
 Observable Symptom in Logs 
 Underlying Root Mechanism 
 Concrete Measurement to Take 
 Corrective Next Step 
 
 
 
 
 Validation Dice on  defect_b  is exactly  \(0.00\) , while train loss converges. 
 Gradient starvation: rare class is absent from most batches; optimizer steps decay weights toward background bias. 
 Measure per-class positive count per epoch; check  positive_dice_b  vs.  dice_mean . 
 Introduce class-balanced Dice reduction or bounded weighted sampling ( \(w_{\max} \le 4.0\) ). 
 
 
 False alarm rate on clean images surges; clean specificity drops below  \(80\%\) . 
 Prior shift: model was trained on an artificially defect-dense distribution, learning an over-sensitive decision threshold. 
 Compute  fp_rate_on_empty  across classes; evaluate clean-image perfect rate. 
 Reduce sampling weight ceiling ( \(w_{\max}\) ); re-calibrate decision thresholds  \(\tau\)  on natural validation data. 
 
 
 Model achieves high training Dice on rare class, but validation Dice remains near zero. 
 Overfitting through duplicate repetition: the model memorized the few oversampled training strips. 
 Check training vs. validation loss gap on rare-class subset; check gradient norms. 
 Apply stronger spatial augmentations (flips, contrast jitter); cap sampling weight; increase weight decay. 
 
 
 Training loss diverges to  NaN  or spikes erratically. 
 Excessive positive loss weight ( pos_weight > 50 ) produces massive gradient explosions on rare pixel errors. 
 Inspect  train/gradient_norm  and individual loss terms ( bce_b ,  dice_b ). 
 Clamp  pos_weight  to a reasonable ceiling (e.g.  \(\le 20.0\) ); enable gradient clipping ( clip_grad_norm_ ). 
 
 
 
 
 6. Implementation Pattern: Bounded Sampling in PyTorch 
 Here is how to construct a bounded, leakage-free  WeightedRandomSampler  in PyTorch: 
 import numpy as np
import torch
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, WeightedRandomSampler

def build_bounded_sampler(
    train_records: list[dict],
    max_weight: float = 4.0,
    seed: int = 42
) -> WeightedRandomSampler:
    """Constructs a deterministic WeightedRandomSampler with bounded square-root weights."""
    n_records = len(train_records)
    # Binary presence array: shape [N, 4]
    presence = np.array([r["active_defects"] for r in train_records], dtype=bool)

    # Class prevalence rates clamped to at least 1/N
    rates = np.maximum(presence.mean(axis=0), 1.0 / n_records)

    # Sqrt inverse class weights capped at max_weight
    class_weights = np.clip(1.0 / np.sqrt(rates), 1.0, max_weight)

    # Assign weight to each image
    sample_weights = np.ones(n_records, dtype=np.float64)
    for i, r in enumerate(train_records):
        active_classes = [c for c, is_active in enumerate(r["active_defects"]) if is_active]
        if active_classes:
            # Use the max class weight to avoid double-counting multi-defect images
            sample_weights[i] = np.max([class_weights[c] for c in active_classes])

    generator = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    return WeightedRandomSampler(
        weights=torch.tensor(sample_weights, dtype=torch.double),
        num_samples=n_records,
        replacement=True,
        generator=generator
    ) 
 
 [!WARNING]
 Strict Validation Invariant :
The  WeightedRandomSampler  must  ONLY  be applied to the  train_loader . The  val_loader  must  ALWAYS  use standard sequential or unweighted loading ( shuffle=False ,  sampler=None ). Altering the validation distribution invalidates your evaluation metrics! 
 
 
 7. Common Pitfalls Checklist 
 
 The Validation Oversampling Trap : 
 Mistake : Applying the weighted sampler to the entire dataset before splitting, or evaluating validation metrics on an oversampled validation loader. 
 Consequence : Validation score appears high because rare defects are overrepresented, but fails completely on Kaggle's natural test distribution. 
 
 
 Double-Counting Multi-Label Images : 
 Mistake : Multiplying class weights ( \(w_i = w_A \times w_B \times w_C\) ) for images with multiple defects. 
 Consequence : Rare multi-defect images receive astronomical weights (e.g.,  \(w_i = 120.0\) ), causing the optimizer to overfit exclusively to those few strips. 
 
 
 Ignoring Clean Image Specificity : 
 Mistake : Celebrating an increase in  positive_dice_b  from 0.00 to 0.45 without checking whether  clean_image_perfect_rate  dropped from 95% to 50%. 
 Consequence : The official competition score drops because false-positive penalties outweigh the rare-class gain.

title: Guide 02 · LR Schedulers & Warmup
text:
Learning-Rate Schedulers and Warmup Strategies 
 In deep learning optimization, the  learning rate ( \(\eta\) )  is universally recognized as the single most critical hyperparameter. It dictates the magnitude of parameter updates across the high-dimensional loss surface.  
 In industrial anomaly segmentation—where networks pair deep pretrained feature extractors with randomly initialized decoders to detect millimeter-thin defects—a static, constant learning rate is rarely sufficient. A learning rate aggressive enough to escape poor initial local minima early in training will cause weights to oscillate chaotically around the sharp, narrow ravines required to trace hairline defect boundaries later in training. 
 This guide explores the physical and geometric role of learning-rate dynamics, contrasts standard schedule archetypes, analyzes the stabilization mechanics of linear warmup, examines per-batch versus per-epoch stepping cadences, and provides a structured protocol for controlled schedule comparisons. 
 
 1. Observable Problem: Destabilization and Late-Stage Oscillation 
 Consider two diagnostic traces from segmentation runs using a constant learning rate  \(\eta = 10^{-3}\) : 
 Run A: Initial Destabilization (No Warmup)
Epoch 1: Train Loss = 0.842 | Gradient Norm = 142.8 | Val Foreground Dice = 0.08
Epoch 2: Train Loss = 1.620 | Gradient Norm = 380.2 | Val Foreground Dice = 0.00
Epoch 3: Train Loss = 0.910 | Gradient Norm = 95.4  | Val Foreground Dice = 0.12
Symptom: Large initial gradients from the random decoder shatter pretrained encoder weights,
causing loss spikes and unstable early representations.

Run B: Late-Stage Oscillation (Constant Learning Rate)
Epoch 15: Train Loss = 0.185 | Val Foreground Dice = 0.582
Epoch 20: Train Loss = 0.182 | Val Foreground Dice = 0.579
Epoch 25: Train Loss = 0.184 | Val Foreground Dice = 0.581
Epoch 30: Train Loss = 0.181 | Val Foreground Dice = 0.578
Symptom: Training loss and validation Dice plateau prematurely. The constant step size
overshoots the fine, sharp minima needed to resolve subtle scratch boundaries. 
 Both failure modes highlight the fundamental limitation of a fixed learning rate:  the optimal step size at the start of training is drastically different from the optimal step size near convergence . 
 
 2. Optimization Mechanics: The Role of the Learning Rate 
 In stochastic gradient descent with momentum and AdamW, parameter updates follow the general form: 
 \[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta_t \cdot \hat{m}_t\] 
 where  \(\theta_t\)  represents the model weights at step  \(t\) ,  \(\eta_t\)  is the instantaneous learning rate, and  \(\hat{m}_t\)  is the bias-corrected gradient vector (or momentum-scaled directional estimate). 
 The optimization trajectory encounters three distinct phases during a training run: 
 Phase 1: Exploration & Alignment (Epochs 1 to 5)
• Gradients are large and noisy.
• Randomly initialized decoder weights must align with pretrained encoder features.
• Risk: Gradient explosions shattering pretrained representations.
• Need: Low, gradually increasing learning rate (Linear Warmup).

Phase 2: Active Traversal (Epochs 5 to 20)
• Model descends the primary valleys of the loss surface.
• Coarse defect patterns, class shapes, and major spatial features are learned.
• Need: High, sustained learning rate to make steady progress and escape saddle points.

Phase 3: Fine Boundary Annealing (Epochs 20 to 30)
• Coarse features are established; optimization focuses on sub-pixel boundary refinement.
• Minima for thin scratches (2–5 pixels wide) are steep and narrow.
• Need: Smooth decay to a fraction of the initial learning rate (1% to 5%) to settle into narrow minima. 
 
 3. Schedule Archetypes: Mathematical Formulation 
 
 Figure 2.1: Comparison of learning-rate trajectories across a 30-epoch budget. Warmup followed by Cosine Annealing provides smooth, continuous decay down to the minimum learning-rate floor. 
 1. Step Decay ( StepLR  /  MultiStepLR ) 
 Multiplies the learning rate by a fixed factor  \(\gamma \in (0, 1)\)  at pre-determined epoch milestones: 
 \[\eta_t = \eta_0 \cdot \gamma^{\lfloor t / s \rfloor}\] 
 where  \(s\)  is the step size (e.g., decay every 10 epochs by  \(\gamma = 0.2\) ). 
 
 Advantage : Simple and intuitive. 
 Disadvantage : Discontinuous drops introduce abrupt shocks to optimizer momentum buffers; requires manual tuning of step milestone epochs. 
 
 2. Cosine Annealing ( CosineAnnealingLR ) 
 Introduced by Loshchilov and Hutter (2016), cosine annealing smoothly decreases the learning rate following a half-cosine wave: 
 \[\eta_t = \eta_{\min} + \frac{1}{2} (\eta_{\max} - \eta_{\min}) \left( 1 + \cos\left( \frac{\pi t}{T_{\max}} \right) \right)\] 
 where: 
 
 \(\eta_{\max}\) : Peak learning rate (e.g.,  \(10^{-3}\) ). 
 \(\eta_{\min}\) : Minimum learning rate floor (e.g.,  \(10^{-5}\)  or  \(0.01 \times \eta_{\max}\) ). 
 \(t\) : Current optimization step or epoch. 
 
 \(T_{\max}\) : Total number of steps or epochs in the training budget. 
 
 
 Advantage : Smooth, non-discontinuous trajectory without hyperparameter milestones. 
 
 Physical Meaning : The early derivative of cosine is near zero, allowing sustained exploration; the middle phase descends rapidly; the final tail flattens smoothly, granting ample time for delicate boundary annealing. 
 
 3. Validation-Driven Plateau Decay ( ReduceLROnPlateau ) 
 Instead of following a predetermined clock, this scheduler dynamically monitors a validation metric (such as validation loss or validation Foreground Dice): 
 \[\eta_{k+1} = \begin{cases} 
\eta_k \cdot \gamma & \text{if validation metric has not improved by } \delta_{\min} \text{ for } p \text{ epochs} \\
\eta_k & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}\] 
 where  \(p\)  is patience (e.g., 3 epochs) and  \(\gamma\)  is the reduction factor (e.g., 0.5). 
 
 Advantage : Highly responsive to actual model progress; pauses decay if the model is still learning. 
 Disadvantage : Sensitive to validation metric noise. If rare defect sampling causes validation Dice to fluctuate, the scheduler may prematurely drop the learning rate to zero. 
 
 
 4. The Critical Role of Linear Warmup 
 In modern segmentation architectures, the encoder backbone is typically pre-trained on ImageNet (millions of natural images), while the decoder, skip-connection projections, and segmentation head are initialized with random Gaussian noise. 
 If training commences immediately at maximum learning rate ( \(\eta_{\max} = 10^{-3}\) ): 
 
 The random decoder outputs wildly inaccurate predictions, generating massive loss values. 
 Backpropagating these massive initial losses produces violent gradient updates across all layers. 
 These updates shatter the delicate, pre-trained spatial feature detectors in early encoder convolutions. 
 
 The Linear Warmup Formulation: 
 Over the first  \(E_{\text{warmup}}\)  epochs (typically 2 to 5 epochs): 
 \[\eta_t = \eta_{\max} \cdot \left( \frac{t + 1}{E_{\text{warmup}}} \right), \quad \text{for } 0 \le t < E_{\text{warmup}}\] 
 During warmup: 
 
 Initial gradients are scaled down proportionally ( \(1/3\) ,  \(2/3\) , then  \(3/3\) ). 
 The randomly initialized decoder adjusts its weights into a plausible range. 
 Batch Normalization running statistics stabilize without corrupting backbone feature representations. 
 
 
 5. Stepping Cadence: Per-Batch vs. Per-Epoch 
 A common source of confusion is whether  scheduler.step()  should be invoked after  every training mini-batch  or once at the  end of each epoch . 
 Cadence A: Per-Epoch Stepping
• Scheduler is called once after all training batches in the epoch complete.
• Total schedule length: T_max = num_epochs (e.g., T_max = 30).
• Common for: StepLR, ReduceLROnPlateau, basic LambdaLR.

Cadence B: Per-Batch Stepping
• Scheduler is called after EVERY optimizer step (every batch or accumulation group).
• Total schedule length: T_max = num_epochs * steps_per_epoch.
  Example: 30 epochs * 285 batches = 8,550 total steps.
• Common for: OneCycleLR, fine-grained CosineAnnealingLR. 
 
 [!CAUTION]
 The Cadence Mismatch Trap :
If you configure  CosineAnnealingLR(optimizer, T_max=30)  intending it for 30 epochs, but accidentally call  scheduler.step()  inside your inner training loop after every batch, the scheduler will complete its entire 30-epoch decay in the  first 30 batches of Epoch 1 ! The remaining 29 epochs will run at the flat minimum learning rate. 
 
 
 6. Implementation Pattern: AdamW with Warmup and Cosine Decay 
 Here is the clean, reproducible PyTorch implementation using  torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR : 
 import math
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.optim import AdamW
from torch.optim.lr_scheduler import LambdaLR

def build_warmup_cosine_scheduler(
    optimizer: torch.optim.Optimizer,
    epochs: int,
    warmup_epochs: int = 3,
    min_lr_ratio: float = 0.01,
) -> LambdaLR:
    """Creates a per-epoch LambdaLR scheduler combining linear warmup with cosine decay.

    Args:
        optimizer: PyTorch optimizer (e.g. AdamW).
        epochs: Total training budget in epochs.
        warmup_epochs: Number of initial epochs dedicated to linear warmup.
        min_lr_ratio: Minimum LR floor expressed as a fraction of initial LR (e.g. 0.01 = 1%).
    """
    def lr_lambda(epoch: int) -> float:
        # Phase 1: Linear Warmup
        if epoch < warmup_epochs:
            return float(epoch + 1) / max(1, warmup_epochs)

        # Phase 2: Cosine Annealing Decay
        progress = float(epoch - warmup_epochs) / max(1, epochs - warmup_epochs - 1)
        progress = min(1.0, max(0.0, progress))
        cosine_decay = 0.5 * (1.0 + math.cos(math.pi * progress))

        return min_lr_ratio + (1.0 - min_lr_ratio) * cosine_decay

    return LambdaLR(optimizer, lr_lambda) 
 Complete Training Step Loop Sequence: 
 # Setup
optimizer = AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
scheduler = build_warmup_cosine_scheduler(optimizer, epochs=30, warmup_epochs=3)

for epoch in range(30):
    model.train()
    for batch in train_loader:
        optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        images, masks = batch["image"].to(device), batch["mask"].to(device)

        loss = criterion(model(images), masks)
        loss.backward()

        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
        optimizer.step()  # Optimizer MUST step before scheduler

    # Validation step
    val_metrics = evaluate(model, val_loader)

    # Step per-epoch scheduler at epoch boundary
    scheduler.step()

    current_lr = optimizer.param_groups[0]["lr"]
    print(f"Epoch {epoch+1:02d} Complete | Val Foreground Dice: {val_metrics['fg_dice']:.4f} | Next LR: {current_lr:.2e}") 
 
 7. Diagnostic Symptoms: Causes and Checks 
 
 
 
 Observable Symptom in Logs 
 Underlying Root Cause 
 Verification Check 
 Recommended Next Step 
 
 
 
 
 Loss diverges to  NaN  in Epoch 1, especially when starting with pretrained backbone. 
 Gradient shattering: high initial LR applied to random decoder propagates unstable gradients into encoder. 
 Check  train/gradient_norm  in first 50 steps; inspect decoder weight initialization. 
 Add 3–5 epochs of linear warmup; verify initial learning rate  \(\le 10^{-3}\) ; add gradient clipping. 
 
 
 Learning rate drops to minimum floor before Epoch 1 finishes. 
 Cadence mismatch: per-epoch scheduler ( T_max = 30 ) was stepped inside the per-batch inner loop. 
 Print  optimizer.param_groups[0]['lr']  at every batch; inspect scheduler call location. 
 Move  scheduler.step()  outside the batch loop to the epoch boundary. 
 
 
 Training loss continues descending smoothly, but validation Dice stops improving at epoch 12. 
 Overfitting on training distribution; model memorizing subtle texture patterns without generalizable boundary rules. 
 Compare training loss vs. validation loss curve; inspect validation error masks. 
 Introduce learning rate decay (cosine); add early stopping; increase data augmentations. 
 
 
 ReduceLROnPlateau  drops learning rate prematurely on epoch 4 during noisy validation. 
 Patience window too short ( \(p = 1\) ), causing scheduler to react to normal validation mini-batch stochasticity. 
 Check validation Dice variance across consecutive epochs. 
 Increase patience to  \(p \ge 4\) ; enforce  min_delta  (e.g.,  \(0.005\) ) to ignore minor noise. 
 
 
 
 
 8. Ungraded "Try It": Schedule Selection Challenge 
 Review the following three project scenarios and determine which schedule configuration is most technically sound: 
 Scenario A:
A student has a fixed budget of 30 epochs on Kaggle GPUs. They are using an EfficientNet-B2
backbone paired with a U-Net++ decoder. They want a smooth, predictable decay that spends
adequate time annealing boundary pixels in the final 10 epochs.

Scenario B:
A student has an open-ended training budget on a private workstation. They are uncertain
how many epochs the model will need to converge, and they want the learning rate to drop
only when validation loss demonstrably flattens for several consecutive evaluations.

Scenario C:
A student trains a model from scratch (randomly initialized encoder and decoder, no ImageNet
weights). They want to ramp up the learning rate immediately to 5e-3 on batch 1. 
 Diagnostic Questions : 
 
 For Scenario A, why is a Linear Warmup (3 epochs) + Cosine Annealing schedule preferable to StepLR? 
 For Scenario B, what monitored quantity and patience setting should be passed to  ReduceLROnPlateau  to avoid premature stopping? 
 For Scenario C, what will happen to the randomly initialized weights if warmup is omitted? 
 
 
 9. Authoritative References 
 
 PyTorch  torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR 
 PyTorch  torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR 
 PyTorch  torch.optim.lr_scheduler.ReduceLROnPlateau 
 Loshchilov, I., & Hutter, F. (2016).  SGDR: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Warm Restarts . ICLR. (Foundational cosine annealing reference). 
 Goyal, P., et al. (2017).  Accurate, Large Minibatch SGD: Training ImageNet in 1 Hour . arXiv:1706.02677. (Foundational linear warmup reference).

title: Guide 03 · Early Stopping & Checkpoints
text:
Early Stopping, Checkpoint Governance, and Validation Drift 
 In an ideal theoretical world, training a neural network would proceed until the training loss reaches zero and the validation metric reaches a smooth, permanent plateau. In real-world industrial surface segmentation, however, the relationship between training loss, validation loss, and task-specific overlap metrics is far more complex. 
 A network trained for too many epochs will inevitably memorize idiosyncratic surface noise, surface reflections, and camera lighting variations, leading to  overfitting . Conversely, halting training too early leaves the model in an  underfitted  state where fine scratch boundaries remain blurred. 
 This guide explores the mechanics of  early stopping , establishes rigorous  checkpoint governance , warns against the subtle hazard of  holdout overfitting (validation drift) , and provides a framework for controlled model selection. 
 
 1. Observable Problem: The Checkpoint Dilemma 
 Consider the following validation history from a 30-epoch training run on a held-out validation fold: 
 Training History Observation:
Epoch 05: Val Loss = 0.420 | Val Foreground Dice = 0.380
Epoch 10: Val Loss = 0.245 | Val Foreground Dice = 0.520
Epoch 14: Val Loss = 0.228 | Val Foreground Dice = 0.565  <-- Minimum Validation Loss!
Epoch 18: Val Loss = 0.235 | Val Foreground Dice = 0.610
Epoch 22: Val Loss = 0.248 | Val Foreground Dice = 0.638  <-- Maximum Foreground Dice!
Epoch 26: Val Loss = 0.285 | Val Foreground Dice = 0.615
Epoch 30: Val Loss = 0.330 | Val Foreground Dice = 0.582  <-- Final Checkpoint (Overfitted) 
 Notice the crucial divergences: 
 
 Loss vs. Metric Divergence : Validation loss reached its minimum at  Epoch 14 , but Foreground Dice continued climbing for another 8 epochs, peaking at  Epoch 22 ! 
 The "Last Checkpoint" Trap : If the student deploys the weights from the final epoch ( Epoch 30 ), their model has already degraded by 5.6 Dice points ( \(0.638 \to 0.582\) ). 
 The "Premature Exit" Trap : If the student stopped training as soon as validation loss ticked upward after Epoch 14, they would have missed the best segmentation checkpoint entirely. 
 
 To manage this, we must formalize early stopping as an explicit, rule-governed system. 
 
 2. Early Stopping Dynamics 
 
 Figure 3.1: Annotated validation trajectory illustrating validation loss minimum versus foreground Dice peak, patience window tolerance, metric noise, and automatic rollback to the best checkpoint. 
 Early stopping is governed by four core parameters: 
 1. The Monitored Quantity ( \(M\) ) 
 What signal determines whether the model is improving? 
 
 Validation Loss : Standard deep learning default, but often misaligned with competition metrics due to well-calibrated background probability creep. 
 Validation Mean Dice ( dice_mean ) : Dangerous due to the "clean-pair inflation trap" (see Guide 05). 
 Validation Foreground Dice ( foreground_dice ) : Evaluates Dice overlap exclusively on ground-truth positive pairs. Highly recommended for checkpoint selection. 
 Competition Weighted Proxy Score : Balances foreground Dice (70%), clean-image false positive penalty (20%), and empty-pair accuracy (10%). 
 
 2. Direction of Improvement ( mode ) 
 
 mode='min' : For loss functions where lower is better ( \(M_{\text{current}} < M_{\text{best}}\) ). 
 mode='max' : For Dice and accuracy metrics where higher is better ( \(M_{\text{current}} > M_{\text{best}}\) ). 
 
 3. Minimum Improvement Delta ( \(\delta_{\min}\) ) 
 Stochastic mini-batch gradient descent introduces natural variance into validation scores. A model whose Dice fluctuates from  \(0.6201\)  to  \(0.6203\)  has not meaningfully improved.
The parameter  \(\delta_{\min}\)  (e.g.,  \(0.002\)  or  \(0.005\) ) acts as a noise filter: 
 \[\text{Improved if: } M_{\text{current}} > M_{\text{best}} + \delta_{\min} \quad (\text{for } \text{mode='max'})\] 
 4. Patience Window ( \(p\) ) 
 The number of consecutive epochs without improvement  \(> \delta_{\min}\)  that training is allowed to continue before being stopped: 
 \[\text{Stale Counter: } s_{t+1} = \begin{cases} 
0 & \text{if } M_t > M_{\text{best}} + \delta_{\min} \\
s_t + 1 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}\] 
 \[\text{Terminate if: } s_{t+1} \ge p\] 
 Typical patience values in surface segmentation range from  \(p = 4\)  to  \(p = 7\)  epochs . A patience window that is too short ( \(p = 1\)  or  \(2\) ) stops prematurely on normal validation noise; a window that is too long ( \(p > 15\) ) wastes expensive GPU compute on an overfitted model. 
 
 3. Checkpoint Governance: The "Last" vs. "Best" Contract 
 A professional training loop maintains two distinct checkpoint files on disk: 
 checkpoints/fold0/
├── last.pt   # Contains state from the MOST RECENT completed epoch (e.g. Epoch 26)
└── best.pt   # Contains state from the HIGHEST SCORING epoch (e.g. Epoch 22) 
 The State Dictionary Contract: 
 A complete checkpoint must contain more than just model weights. To allow seamless resumption and auditing, it must serialize: 
 checkpoint = {
    "epoch": epoch,
    "best_score": best_score,
    "stale_epochs": stale_epochs,
    "selection_metric": "foreground_dice",
    "model_state_dict": model.state_dict(),
    "optimizer_state_dict": optimizer.state_dict(),
    "scheduler_state_dict": scheduler.state_dict(),
    "scaler_state_dict": scaler.state_dict(),  # AMP gradient scaler state
    "rng_state": torch.get_rng_state(),        # For deterministic resumption
    "config": cfg.snapshot(),
} 
 
 [!IMPORTANT]
 Atomic Saving Protocol :
Never overwrite  best.pt  directly. If your process runs out of disk space or is interrupted mid-write,  best.pt  will be corrupted. Always save to a temporary file ( best.pt.tmp ) and perform an atomic filesystem replacement:
 torch.save(checkpoint, "best.pt.tmp")
os.replace("best.pt.tmp", "best.pt") 
 
 
 4. The Holdout Overfitting Hazard (Validation Drift) 
 One of the most insidious traps in competitive machine learning is  overfitting to the validation holdout . 
 The Mechanism of Information Leakage: 
 
 You establish a clean  \(80/20\)  train/validation split (Fold 0). 
 You run 50 experiments: tuning learning rates, testing schedulers, tweaking loss weights, adjusting early stopping patience, and sweeping post-processing thresholds. 
 In every experiment, you select the checkpoint that scores highest on Fold 0. 
 The Consequence : Even though model weights were updated only on training data, your  human decisions  (and early stopping decisions) were updated on Fold 0! 
 Over time, your pipeline selects models that happen to fit the statistical idiosyncrasies of that specific 20% holdout sample. When submitted to the private Kaggle test set, performance drops significantly. 
 
 Defensive Governance: 
 
 
 Multi-Fold Out-of-Fold (OOF) Validation :
   Evaluate decisions across all 5 folds of your combination-stratified split. A training improvement is only genuine if the average 5-fold OOF score increases consistently. 
 
 
 Fixed Protocol Invariants :
   Decide your early stopping metric, threshold grid, and patience  before  running experiments. Do not tweak stopping rules post-hoc to retroactively favor a particular run. 
 
 
 Record All Artifacts :
   Store the exact checkpoint hash ( sha256 ) and training log history with each saved model. 
 
 
 
 5. Diagnostic Symptoms: Causes and Checks 
 
 
 
 Observable Symptom in Logs 
 Root Cause 
 Verification Check 
 Corrective Action 
 
 
 
 
 Training stops at Epoch 3, even though model has barely begun learning. 
 mode  parameter inverted (e.g.  mode='min'  passed for Dice metric), or  min_delta  set excessively high ( \(0.10\) ). 
 Check early stopping initialization logs; verify score comparison logic. 
 Set  mode='max'  for Dice; set  min_delta  to a realistic value ( \(0.002\)  to  \(0.005\) ). 
 
 
 Validation loss increases steadily while Foreground Dice continues climbing. 
 Expected phenomenon: probability calibration drift. The model becomes more confident on easy background pixels, causing BCE loss to rise slightly, but thresholded masks improve. 
 Inspect probability distributions; evaluate Dice vs. Loss curve divergence. 
 Monitor  foreground_dice  or the competition weighted proxy for checkpoint selection, not raw loss. 
 
 
 Model performance on Kaggle test set is far worse than the best validation checkpoint. 
 Holdout overfitting: early stopping selected a noisy outlier epoch that overfit specific validation images. 
 Check validation score standard deviation across folds (OOF); inspect validation predictions. 
 Evaluate 5-fold cross-validation; increase early stopping patience slightly ( \(p = 5\) ); increase regularizing augmentations. 
 
 
 Process crashes mid-save, leaving an unreadable zero-byte  best.pt . 
 Non-atomic file write interrupted by GPU timeout or disk quota exhaustion. 
 Attempt  torch.load('best.pt')  to verify archive integrity. 
 Use the temporary write +  os.replace  atomic saving pattern. 
 
 
 
 
 6. Implementation Pattern: Robust Early Stopping Class 
 Here is a complete, production-grade  EarlyStopping  implementation in PyTorch: 
 import copy
import os
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class EarlyStopping:
    """Manages early stopping logic, patience counting, and atomic checkpoint persistence."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        patience: int = 5,
        min_delta: float = 0.003,
        mode: str = "max",
        checkpoint_path: str = "best.pt",
    ):
        self.patience = patience
        self.min_delta = min_delta
        self.mode = mode
        self.checkpoint_path = checkpoint_path

        self.stale_epochs = 0
        self.best_score = None
        self.best_epoch = 0
        self.should_stop = False

    def step(
        self,
        current_score: float,
        epoch: int,
        model: nn.Module,
        checkpoint_payload: dict,
    ) -> bool:
        """Evaluates current epoch score. Saves checkpoint atomically if score improves."""
        if self.best_score is None:
            self._save_new_best(current_score, epoch, model, checkpoint_payload)
            return True

        if self.mode == "max":
            improved = current_score > (self.best_score + self.min_delta)
        else:
            improved = current_score < (self.best_score - self.min_delta)

        if improved:
            self._save_new_best(current_score, epoch, model, checkpoint_payload)
            self.stale_epochs = 0
            return True
        else:
            self.stale_epochs += 1
            if self.stale_epochs >= self.patience:
                self.should_stop = True
            return False

    def _save_new_best(self, score: float, epoch: int, model: nn.Module, payload: dict):
        self.best_score = score
        self.best_epoch = epoch

        # Inject model state into payload
        payload["model_state_dict"] = model.state_dict()
        payload["best_score"] = score
        payload["epoch"] = epoch

        # Atomic file write
        tmp_path = f"{self.checkpoint_path}.tmp"
        torch.save(payload, tmp_path)
        os.replace(tmp_path, self.checkpoint_path)
        print(f"-> [NEW BEST] Epoch {epoch:02d}: {score:.4f} saved to {self.checkpoint_path}") 
 
 7. Ungraded "Try It": Checkpoint Selection Analysis 
 Examine this fictional training run log: 
 Monitored Metric: Validation Foreground Dice (mode='max')
Patience: 4 epochs | Min Delta: 0.004

Epoch 08: Score = 0.510 (Best: 0.510, Stale: 0) -> New Best
Epoch 09: Score = 0.518 (Best: 0.518, Stale: 0) -> New Best (+0.008 > 0.004)
Epoch 10: Score = 0.520 (Best: 0.518, Stale: 1) -> No significant gain (+0.002 < 0.004)
Epoch 11: Score = 0.517 (Best: 0.518, Stale: 2) -> Score dropped
Epoch 12: Score = 0.523 (Best: 0.523, Stale: 0) -> New Best (+0.005 > 0.004)
Epoch 13: Score = 0.525 (Best: 0.523, Stale: 1) -> No significant gain (+0.002 < 0.004)
Epoch 14: Score = 0.521 (Best: 0.523, Stale: 2)
Epoch 15: Score = 0.519 (Best: 0.523, Stale: 3)
Epoch 16: Score = 0.520 (Best: 0.523, Stale: 4) -> Early stopping triggered! 
 Diagnostic Questions : 
 
 At Epoch 10, the score rose from  \(0.518\)  to  \(0.520\) . Why did the stale counter increase from 0 to 1 instead of resetting? 
 Which epoch's model weights reside in  best.pt  when training terminates at Epoch 16? 
 If the student set  patience = 2 , at which epoch would training have been prematurely aborted, and what peak score would have been lost? 
 
 
 8. Authoritative References 
 
 Prechelt, L. (1998).  Early Stopping — But When?  Neural Networks: Tricks of the Trade, Springer. (Seminal paper formalizing patience and stopping criteria). 
 PyTorch  Checkpointing Tutorial 
 Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R., & Friedman, J. (2009).  The Elements of Statistical Learning , Chapter 7: Model Assessment and Selection. (Information leakage and validation overfitting).

title: Guide 04 · Mixed Precision (AMP) & Memory
text:
Mixed Precision (AMP) and GPU Memory Optimization 
 Deep segmentation networks operating on high-resolution industrial strips ( \(128 \times 800\)  pixels) place intense demands on GPU hardware. As your architectures advance from lightweight baselines to deep encoder-decoder variants with attention gates, GPU video memory (VRAM) rapidly becomes the primary engineering bottleneck. 
 An unoptimized pipeline will trigger abrupt  CUDA out of memory  (OOM) crashes, force you to train with artificially tiny batches, or waste hours waiting on memory-bandwidth-bound matrix multiplications.  
 This guide breaks down the physical anatomy of GPU memory, explains the numerical mechanics of  Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP)  in PyTorch 2.x, details dynamic gradient scaling, and demonstrates how to decouple physical memory constraints from optimization dynamics using  gradient accumulation . 
 
 1. Observable Problem: The OOM Crash and the Throughput Bottleneck 
 Consider two common runtime errors encountered when expanding segmentation training: 
 Crash 1: The Out-Of-Memory Abortion
RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 400.00 MiB (GPU 0; 15.78 GiB total capacity; 
14.92 GiB already allocated; 312.50 MiB free; 15.10 GiB reserved in total by PyTorch)
Symptom: The training loop crashes abruptly mid-epoch when trying to allocate intermediate activation
tensors for a high-resolution skip connection.

Bottleneck 2: The Underutilized GPU
Batch Size: 2 | GPU Allocation: 3.2 GiB / 16 GiB | GPU Compute Utilization: 22%
Epoch Time: 18 minutes (Throughput: 10.5 samples/second)
Symptom: Memory is kept small to avoid OOM, but the GPU's Tensor Cores sit idle, waiting on memory-bandwidth
transfers of standard 32-bit floating-point tensors. 
 To resolve both challenges, we must understand exactly where GPU bytes are spent during forward and backward passes. 
 
 2. Anatomy of GPU Memory: Where Do the Gigabytes Go? 
 
 Figure 4.1: The main categories of training memory. The widths are illustrative, not measured proportions; profile your own model and batch size. 
 GPU memory during training is partitioned into five distinct categories: 
 1. Model Parameters (Weights) 
 For a network with  \(M\)  parameters stored in standard single-precision float32 (4 bytes per parameter): 
 \[\text{Memory}_{\text{weights}} = M \times 4\text{ bytes}\] 
 
 A 10-million parameter U-Net requires  \(10^7 \times 4 = 40\text{ MB}\) . 
 An 80-million parameter modern backbone requires  \(80 \times 10^6 \times 4 = 320\text{ MB}\) . 
 Takeaway : Contrary to popular belief, raw model parameters occupy a relatively modest portion of modern GPU memory. 
 
 2. Parameter Gradients 
 During the backward pass, PyTorch computes a partial derivative  \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta}\)  for every trainable parameter  \(\theta\) : 
 \[\text{Memory}_{\text{gradients}} = M \times 4\text{ bytes}\] 
 
 Matches parameter memory exactly: a 10M parameter model requires another  \(40\text{ MB}\) . 
 
 3. Optimizer State (The Silent Memory Consumer) 
 Adaptive optimizers like  AdamW  maintain two internal running averages for every single parameter: 
 
 First moment vector  \(m_t\)  (momentum):  \(M \times 4\text{ bytes}\) . 
 Second moment vector  \(v_t\)  (uncentered variance):  \(M \times 4\text{ bytes}\) . 
 
 \[\text{Memory}_{\text{AdamW}} = 2 \times M \times 4 = 8 \times M\text{ bytes}\] 
 
 For a 10M parameter model, AdamW consumes  \(80\text{ MB}\)  of VRAM—twice the size of the model itself! 
 For a 50M parameter model, AdamW consumes  \(400\text{ MB}\)  purely for its momentum tracking buffers. 
 
 4. Activations (The Dominant Memory Consumer in Segmentation) 
 During the forward pass, PyTorch must store the intermediate feature maps output by every convolutional and normalization layer so they can be referenced during backpropagation.
The activation footprint scales with: 
 \[\text{Memory}_{\text{activations}} \propto \text{Batch Size } (B) \times \text{Height } (H) \times \text{Width } (W) \times \text{Channels } (C) \times \text{Depth}\] 
 
 
 On an industrial line-scan strip ( \(128 \times 800 = 102,400\text{ pixels}\) ), an early encoder feature map with 64 channels stores: 
 \[8 \text{ images} \times 64 \text{ channels} \times 128 \times 800 \times 4\text{ bytes} \approx 209.7\text{ MB}\] 
 for just  one  convolution layer! 
 
 
 Summed across 40+ layers in a full U-Net, activations easily consume  4 to 10 GiB  of VRAM. 
 
 
 5. Workspace and CUDA Context 
 CUDA driver kernels, PyTorch internal memory allocator caches, and cuDNN workspace buffers typically reserve an overhead of  \(500\text{ MB}\)  to  \(1.2\text{ GiB}\) . 
 
 3. Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP): Mechanics and Formats 
 Standard deep learning computations represent real numbers using  IEEE 754 Single Precision (FP32) : 
 
 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, 23 mantissa (fraction) bits (4 bytes). 
 Dynamic range:  \(\approx 10^{-38}\)  to  \(10^{38}\) . 
 
 Modern GPU architectures (NVIDIA Volta, Turing, Ampere, Ada, Hopper) include dedicated hardware units called  Tensor Cores . Tensor Cores perform matrix multiplications at  \(2\times\)  to  \(4\times\)  higher throughput when tensors are represented in 16-bit formats: 
 Floating-Point 16-bit Formats: 
 
 FP16 (Half Precision) : 
 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits, 10 mantissa bits (2 bytes). 
 Dynamic range:  \(\approx 6 \times 10^{-5}\)  to  \(65,504\) . 
 Limitation : Because it has only 5 exponent bits, numbers smaller than  \(6 \times 10^{-5}\)  underflow to zero. 
 
 
 BF16 (Bfloat16 / Brain Floating Point) : 
 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, 7 mantissa bits (2 bytes). 
 Dynamic range: identical to FP32 ( \(\approx 10^{-38}\)  to  \(10^{38}\) ), but lower precision. 
 Supported natively on Ampere+ (A100, RTX 3000/4000) and modern CPUs. 
 
 
 
 What AMP Does Automatically: 
 PyTorch's Automatic Mixed Precision ( torch.amp ) automatically converts operations: 
 
 Fast 16-bit operations :  \(3 \times 3\)  convolutions,  \(1 \times 1\)  projections, matrix multiplications, and linear layers are executed in FP16/BF16 on Tensor Cores. 
 Protected 32-bit operations : Numerically sensitive operations that require wide dynamic range—such as Batch Normalization statistics, Softmax denominators, and Loss reductions—are automatically retained in FP32. 
 
 
 4. Dynamic Gradient Scaling ( GradScaler ) 
 In FP16, the minimum representable positive number before underflow is  \(\approx 6 \times 10^{-5}\) .
During backpropagation through a deep segmentation network, gradients in early convolutional layers are often very small (e.g.,  \(10^{-6}\)  or  \(10^{-7}\) ). If backpropagated in raw FP16, these gradients  underflow to absolute zero , completely halting weight updates in early encoder layers! 
 To prevent underflow, PyTorch utilizes a  Dynamic Gradient Scaler ( torch.amp.GradScaler ) : 
 Forward Pass:
1. Inputs converted to FP16 inside torch.amp.autocast.
2. Loss computed in FP32 for numerical stability.

Backward Pass:
3. Loss is multiplied by a large scale factor S (e.g., S = 65,536.0):
   Scaled Loss = Loss * S
4. Backpropagation runs on Scaled Loss. All gradients are scaled up by S:
   Scaled Gradients = Gradients * S  (Safe from underflow!)

Optimizer Step:
5. Scaler UNSCALES gradients before the optimizer steps:
   True Gradients = Scaled Gradients / S
6. If any gradient contains Inf or NaN (overflow occurred):
   -> Optimizer step is SKIPPED entirely.
   -> Scale factor S is halved (e.g. 65,536 -> 32,768).
7. If no overflow occurs for N consecutive steps:
   -> Scale factor S is doubled. 
 
 5. Microbatch Sizing and Gradient Accumulation 
 What if your model still exceeds VRAM even with AMP enabled?
Do not immediately resize your images to  \(256 \times 256\)  (which destroys the  \(6.25:1\)  industrial aspect ratio) or shrink your model capacity. Instead, decouple your  hardware microbatch size  from your  effective optimization batch size  using  gradient accumulation . 
 
 Figure 4.2: Step-by-step lifecycle of gradient accumulation. Gradients from 4 microbatches of size 4 accumulate into parameter buffers, achieving an effective batch size of 16 before a single optimizer step is executed. 
 Definitions: 
 
 Microbatch Size ( \(B_{\text{micro}}\) ) : The number of images fed into the GPU in a single  forward()  pass (constrained by physical VRAM). 
 Accumulation Steps ( \(K_{\text{accum}}\) ) : The number of microbatches evaluated before calling  optimizer.step() . 
 
 Effective Batch Size ( \(B_{\text{eff}}\) ) : 
 \[B_{\text{eff}} = B_{\text{micro}} \times K_{\text{accum}}\] 
 
 
 The Loss Scaling Requirement: 
 Because PyTorch's  loss.backward()   accumulates  (sums) gradients into  .grad  buffers, you must divide the loss by  \(K_{\text{accum}}\) : 
 \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{scaled}} = \frac{\mathcal{L}}{K_{\text{accum}}}\] 
 If you forget this division, your accumulated gradients will be  \(K_{\text{accum}}\)  times too large, acting like an unintended  \(K\times\)  spike in your learning rate! 
 
 6. Implementation Pattern: PyTorch 2.x Modern AMP Syntax 
 In this repository, we run  PyTorch 2.8.0 . Modern PyTorch 2.x standardizes mixed precision under the  torch.amp  namespace rather than the legacy  torch.cuda.amp  module. 
 import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.optim import AdamW

# 1. Device and Scaler Initialization
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
amp_enabled = (device.type == "cuda")

# PyTorch 2.x GradScaler constructor takes device_type as first argument
scaler = torch.amp.GradScaler(device.type, enabled=amp_enabled)
optimizer = AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)

# Batch parameters
microbatch_size = 4
accumulation_steps = 4  # Effective batch = 16

optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)

for step, batch in enumerate(train_loader):
    images = batch["image"].to(device, non_blocking=True)
    masks = batch["mask"].to(device, non_blocking=True)

    # 2. Forward pass inside autocast context
    with torch.amp.autocast(device_type=device.type, enabled=amp_enabled):
        logits = model(images)
        loss = criterion(logits, masks)
        # Scale loss by accumulation steps
        scaled_loss = loss / accumulation_steps

    # 3. Scaled backward pass
    scaler.scale(scaled_loss).backward()

    # 4. Optimizer update every `accumulation_steps`
    if (step + 1) % accumulation_steps == 0 or (step + 1) == len(train_loader):
        # A. Unscale gradients before clipping norms
        scaler.unscale_(optimizer)

        # B. Clip gradients
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)

        # C. Step optimizer through scaler
        scaler.step(optimizer)

        # D. Update scaler factor
        scaler.update()

        # E. Zero gradients using set_to_none=True to release memory
        optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) 
 
 [!CAUTION]
 The Unscaling Ordering Rule :
You  MUST  call  scaler.unscale_(optimizer)   BEFORE  calling  torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_() . If you clip gradients before unscaling, PyTorch will evaluate gradient norms on the scaled values ( \(G \times S\) ), misinterpreting healthy gradients as massive explosions and artificially shrinking your updates to zero! 
 
 
 7. Diagnostic Symptoms: Causes and Checks 
 
 
 
 Observable Symptom in Logs 
 Underlying Mechanism 
 Diagnostic Check 
 Corrective Action 
 
 
 
 
 RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory  during validation or test inference. 
 Memory retained by computation graph; or validation run with gradient tracking enabled. 
 Check if validation loop is wrapped in  @torch.inference_mode()  or  with torch.no_grad(): . 
 Use  @torch.inference_mode() ; delete large probability tensors when finished; call  torch.cuda.empty_cache() . 
 
 
 Loss suddenly becomes  NaN  or  Inf  on step 15, and never recovers. 
 Numerical underflow/overflow in loss calculation or logit exponentiation. 
 Print min/max logits; check loss function head consistency. 
 Verify loss calculates BCE on raw logits (not sigmoided probabilities); verify  GradScaler  is active. 
 
 
 Optimizer step appears to be skipped repeatedly; model parameters do not change. 
 GradScaler repeatedly encountering Inf/NaN, triggering automatic step abortion. 
 Inspect  scaler.get_scale() ; if scale factor drops below 1.0, severe numerical overflow is occurring. 
 Clamp loss weights; reduce learning rate; check for zero-division in custom loss denominators. 
 
 
 Training runs  \(3\times\)  slower with AMP enabled than expected. 
 Excessive host-to-device synchronization calls inside the training loop. 
 Search code for  .item() ,  .cpu() , or  print(loss)  inside the per-batch inner loop. 
 Remove intermediate  .item()  calls from GPU; accumulate metrics as tensors and synchronize once per epoch. 
 
 
 
 
 8. Ungraded "Try It": Memory Footprint Estimation

 System Parameters : 
 
 Model parameters ( \(M\) ):  \(21.3 \times 10^6\) 
 Optimizer: AdamW 
 Image resolution:  \(128 \times 800\)  pixels (single-channel grayscale input, 4 output mask channels)

 Questions to Calculate : 
 
 How much memory do the model parameters and gradients occupy in FP32? 
 How much memory does the AdamW optimizer state occupy in FP32? 
 If each strip requires approximately  \(120\text{ MB}\)  of intermediate activations across all U-Net layers during forward propagation at  \(B=1\) , what is the activation memory footprint at  \(B=8\)  in pure FP32? 
 How does enabling PyTorch AMP reduce the activation memory footprint, and how many microbatches of size 4 would be needed to simulate an effective batch size of 16?
