title: Guide 05 · Metric Governance & Overfitting
text:
Metric Governance: Validation Dice, Empty Pairs, and Overfitting 
 In computer vision competitions, the gap between local validation scores and leaderboard reality is the most frequent source of student frustration. A student might excitedly report:  "My validation Dice reached 0.89!" —only to submit their predictions and receive a disappointing leaderboard score of 0.42. 
 How can a model achieve a local Dice of 0.89 and yet fail on the competition leaderboard? The answer lies in the  mathematical mechanics of empty masks  and the  composition of the official competition metric . 
 This guide unravels the "Naive Dice Trap," decomposes the 70/20/10 competition evaluation formula, maps out six diagnostic learning curve archetypes, and establishes strict metric governance to detect overfitting before submitting. 
 
 1. Observable Problem: The "Naive Dice Trap" 
 To understand why aggregate validation numbers can be wildly misleading, examine this mathematical paradox: 
 Suppose you write a "lazy" baseline script that ignores all input images and outputs an  empty prediction (all zeros)  for every defect channel across the entire validation dataset. 
 What is the resulting Dice score? 
 Dataset Setup:
Validation Set: 2,000 image strips x 4 defect classes = 8,000 image-class pairs.
Defect Distribution:
• 1,200 pairs contain real defects (GT Positive: |Y| > 0).
• 6,800 pairs are completely clean (GT Empty: |Y| = 0).

Lazy Model Output: All Zeros (|P| = 0 for all 8,000 pairs).

Scoring the 8,000 pairs using the standard Kaggle empty-pair convention:
1. For the 1,200 positive pairs:
   Prediction is empty -> Dice = (2 * 0) / (0 + |Y|) = 0.00
2. For the 6,800 clean pairs:
   Both GT and Prediction are empty -> Convention defines Dice = 1.00!

Aggregate Naive Mean Dice:
Dice_mean = ( (1,200 * 0.00) + (6,800 * 1.00) ) / 8,000 = 6,800 / 8,000 = 0.8500! 
 
 [!CAUTION]
 The Naive Dice Trap :
A model that predicts  nothing at all  achieves an  \(85\%\)  Naive Mean Dice score! If you monitor  dice_mean  during training, an untrained model that predicts all background will appear to outperform a real model that detects defects but occasionally makes false alarms on clean material. 
 
 
 2. Deconstructing the Evaluation Metric: The 2×2 Contingency Grid 
 To prevent this distortion, we must examine the  contingency grid of image-class pairs : 
 
 Figure 5.1: The 2×2 contingency matrix of image-class pairs. When both ground truth and predictions are empty (Quadrant 4), the score convention assigns 1.0, diluting naive averages. True segmentation capability lives in Quadrant 1 and Quadrant 2. 
 For any individual image  \(i\)  and defect channel  \(c\) : 
 \[\text{Dice}(P, Y) = \begin{cases} 
1.0 & \text{if } |P| = 0 \text{ and } |Y| = 0 \text{ (True Negative Clean Pair)} \\
0.0 & \text{if } |P| > 0 \text{ and } |Y| = 0 \text{ (False Positive Pair)} \\
0.0 & \text{if } |P| = 0 \text{ and } |Y| > 0 \text{ (False Negative Missed Defect)} \\
\frac{2 \sum (P \cap Y)}{\sum P + \sum Y} & \text{if } |P| > 0 \text{ and } |Y| > 0 \text{ (True Positive Overlap)}
\end{cases}\] 
 The Three True Operational Metrics: 
 Instead of relying on a single naive average, professional segmentation pipelines track three separate quantities: 
 1. Foreground Dice ( foreground_dice ) 
 Evaluates Dice overlap  exclusively on ground-truth positive pairs  ( \(|Y| > 0\) ): 
 \[\text{Dice}_{\text{FG}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|} \sum_{(i, c) \in \mathcal{P}} \text{Dice}(P_{i, c}, Y_{i, c})\] 
 where  \(\mathcal{P} = \{ (i, c) \mid |Y_{i, c}| > 0 \}\)  is the set of positive pairs. 
 
 On our "lazy all-zeros model":  \(\text{Dice}_{\text{FG}} = \mathbf{0.0000}\)  (Revealing true failure!). 
 
 2. Empty-Pair Specificity ( empty_pair_accuracy ) 
 Evaluates the model's ability to stay completely silent on clean material ( \(|Y| = 0\) ): 
 \[\text{Spec}_{\text{empty}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{E}|} \sum_{(i, c) \in \mathcal{E}} \mathbb{I}(|P_{i, c}| = 0)\] 
 where  \(\mathcal{E} = \{ (i, c) \mid |Y_{i, c}| = 0 \}\)  is the set of empty pairs. 
 3. False-Positive Pixel Penalty ( false_positive_pixel_score ) 
 Penalizes the total canvas area of hallucinated defect pixels on clean material: 
 \[\text{Score}_{\text{FP-pixels}} = 1.0 - \frac{1}{|\mathcal{E}|} \sum_{(i, c) \in \mathcal{E}} \frac{|P_{i, c}|}{\text{Canvas Pixels}}\] 
 where  \(\text{Canvas Pixels} = 128 \times 800 = 102,400\) . 
 
 3. The Official 70/20/10 Competition Score Architecture 
 The official competition leaderboard score balances detection overlap against false alarm suppression using a weighted composite formula: 
 \[\text{Competition Score} = 0.70 \times \text{Foreground Dice} + 0.20 \times \text{False-Positive Pixel Score} + 0.10 \times \text{Empty-Pair Accuracy}\] 
 Let us compute the score for our "lazy all-zeros model" under the true official metric: 
 \[\text{Score}_{\text{lazy}} = (0.70 \times 0.00) + (0.20 \times 1.00) + (0.10 \times 1.00) = 0.00 + 0.20 + 0.10 = \mathbf{0.3000}\] 
 Under the true metric, the lazy model receives an abysmal  \(0.30\) —matching its actual zero-utility reality! 
 Decision Threshold Trade-offs ( \(\tau\) ) 
 Continuous sigmoid probabilities  \(P \in [0, 1]\)  are converted to binary masks via a decision threshold  \(\tau\) : 
 \[\hat{Y}_{i, c} = \mathbb{I}(P_{i, c} \ge \tau)\] 
 
 Lowering  \(\tau\)  (e.g.  \(\tau = 0.3\) ) : Increases sensitivity. Catches faint, low-contrast scratches (raising  \(\text{Dice}_{\text{FG}}\) ), but causes minor surface noise to be classified as defects, devastating  \(\text{Spec}_{\text{empty}}\)  and  \(\text{Score}_{\text{FP}}\) . 
 Raising  \(\tau\)  (e.g.  \(\tau = 0.7\) ) : Increases specificity. Suppresses false alarms on clean material, but misses faint longitudinal micro-cracks. 
 
 Calibrating  \(\tau\)  against the  composite competition score  on held-out validation data is essential before submitting. 
 
 4. Learning Curve Taxonomy: Diagnosing Model Health 
 
 Figure 5.2: Diagnostic taxonomy of deep segmentation learning curves across 25 training epochs, contrasting healthy generalization against overfitting, underfitting, and metric-loss divergence. 
 When monitoring your training and validation curves, watch for these distinct archetypes: 
 Archetype 1: Healthy Generalization 
 
 Symptom : Training loss descends steadily. Validation loss descends in tandem, flattening around Epoch 18. Validation Foreground Dice rises smoothly from  \(0.20\)  to  \(0.64\) . 
 Mechanism : The model is learning robust, invariant features (scratch aspect ratios, inclusion textures) that generalize across unseen strips. 
 Action : Check if a learning-rate scheduler decay can anneal boundaries further; prepare checkpoint for post-processing calibration. 
 
 Archetype 2: Severe Overfitting 
 
 Symptom : Training loss plummets toward near-zero ( \(0.04\) ), while validation loss reaches a minimum at Epoch 8 and surges upward ( \(0.22 \to 0.45\) ). Validation Dice degrades from  \(0.62\)  down to  \(0.51\) . 
 Mechanism : The high-capacity network has memorized specific sensor noise patterns and roller imperfections unique to the training fold. 
 Action : Activate early stopping; increase data augmentation (flips, contrast jitter, CLAHE); increase weight decay; consider dropping model capacity. 
 
 Archetype 3: Severe Underfitting (High Bias) 
 
 Symptom : Both training loss and validation loss flatten early at high values ( \(0.55\) ). Validation Dice remains stagnant below  \(0.25\) . 
 Mechanism : The model lacks capacity or representational power, or the learning rate is trapped in a bad plateau. 
 Action : Verify data loading and target normalization; verify that skip connections are intact; switch to a more expressive backbone; verify loss function heads. 
 
 Archetype 4: Metric-Loss Divergence (Probability Calibration Drift) 
 
 Symptom : Training loss and validation loss both increase slightly, yet Validation Foreground Dice continues rising! 
 Mechanism : The model's raw probability calibration is shifting (predicting higher logits on borderline pixels, incurring BCE penalty), but its rank-ordering remains superior, resulting in cleaner thresholded masks. 
 Action : Do not abort training based on loss alone. Follow the task-specific metric ( foreground_dice ) as your primary checkpoint selection signal. 
 
 
 5. Diagnostic Symptoms: Causes and Checks 
 
 
 
 Observable Symptom in Logs 
 Root Mechanism 
 Concrete Measurement 
 Next Step 
 
 
 
 
 Local validation Dice is  \(0.85+\) , but public leaderboard score is  \(< 0.45\) . 
 The Naive Dice Trap: local code averaged all pairs including true-negative clean pairs ( \(1.0\) ). 
 Compute  foreground_dice  on positive pairs only; evaluate empty-pair false positive count. 
 Switch checkpoint selection and reporting to  foreground_dice  or the 70/20/10 proxy. 
 
 
 Training loss reaches  \(0.05\) , but validation Foreground Dice plateaus at  \(0.35\) . 
 Overfitting to training textures; model memorizing specific strips rather than invariant defect features. 
 Calculate training vs. validation loss gap; inspect training vs. validation predicted masks. 
 Introduce early stopping; increase geometric augmentations (horizontal/vertical flips); increase weight decay. 
 
 
 Validation curves oscillate violently from epoch to epoch (e.g. Dice jumps  \(0.45 \leftrightarrow 0.62\) ). 
 Small validation sample size or severe rare-class variance (the "split lottery"). 
 Check validation fold class support count; verify combination stratification. 
 Ensure validation split uses combination stratification; increase patience  \(p \ge 5\)  to ignore single-epoch jitter. 
 
 
 Best epoch identified by validation loss is completely different from best epoch identified by Dice. 
 BCE loss evaluates soft uncalibrated probabilities, while Dice evaluates thresholded binary decisions. 
 Compare correlation between validation loss and  foreground_dice  across all epochs. 
 Select checkpoints using  foreground_dice  or  score_pair_proxy ; loss is an optimization proxy, not the competition goal. 
 
 
 
 
 6. Implementation Pattern: Logging Comprehensive Validation Metrics 
 Here is how to structure a leak-free validation evaluation function in PyTorch: 
 import numpy as np
import torch

@torch.inference_mode()
def evaluate_validation_run(
    model: torch.nn.Module,
    val_loader: torch.utils.data.DataLoader,
    threshold: float = 0.5,
    device: torch.device = torch.device("cuda"),
) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Computes transparent, leak-free metrics decomposed across positive and clean pairs."""
    model.eval()

    all_dices = []
    all_pred_areas = []
    all_gt_areas = []

    for batch in val_loader:
        images = batch["image"].to(device)
        targets = batch["mask"].cpu().numpy().astype(bool)  # [B, 4, 128, 800]

        logits = model(images)
        probs = torch.sigmoid(logits).cpu().numpy()
        preds = (probs >= threshold)  # [B, 4, 128, 800]

        # Calculate intersection and areas across spatial dimensions (axis 2, 3)
        tp = np.logical_and(preds, targets).sum(axis=(-2, -1))
        pa = preds.sum(axis=(-2, -1))
        ya = targets.sum(axis=(-2, -1))

        total = pa + ya
        # Compute Dice with empty-pair convention = 1.0
        dice = np.divide(2.0 * tp, total, out=np.ones_like(total, dtype=float), where=(total > 0))

        all_dices.append(dice)
        all_pred_areas.append(pa)
        all_gt_areas.append(ya)

    dices = np.concatenate(all_dices, axis=0)       # [N, 4]
    pred_areas = np.concatenate(all_pred_areas, axis=0)
    gt_areas = np.concatenate(all_gt_areas, axis=0)

    # Positive pairs vs. Empty pairs
    is_positive = (gt_areas > 0)
    is_empty = (gt_areas == 0)

    # 1. Naive Mean Dice (For diagnostic awareness only!)
    dice_naive = float(dices.mean())

    # 2. Foreground Dice (Only on positive pairs)
    dice_fg = float(dices[is_positive].mean()) if is_positive.any() else 0.0

    # 3. Clean-Image Specificity (Empty accuracy)
    empty_acc = float((pred_areas[is_empty] == 0).mean()) if is_empty.any() else 1.0

    # 4. FP Pixel Score
    canvas_pixels = 128 * 800
    fp_pixel_score = float(1.0 - (pred_areas[is_empty] / canvas_pixels).mean()) if is_empty.any() else 1.0

    # 5. Official Competition Proxy Score
    competition_proxy = (0.70 * dice_fg) + (0.20 * fp_pixel_score) + (0.10 * empty_acc)

    return {
        "val/naive_mean_dice": dice_naive,
        "val/foreground_dice": dice_fg,
        "val/empty_pair_accuracy": empty_acc,
        "val/fp_pixel_score": fp_pixel_score,
        "val/competition_proxy": competition_proxy,
    } 
 
 7. Ungraded "Try It": Interpreting a Metric Report 
 A student shares the following metric table from their latest validation evaluation: 
 Validation Report:
• Naive Mean Dice: 0.8842
• Foreground Dice: 0.4120
• Empty-Pair Accuracy (Specificity): 0.9650
• False-Positive Pixel Score: 0.9980
• Official Competition Proxy: 0.6811 
 Diagnostic Questions : 
 
 Why is  Naive Mean Dice  ( \(0.8842\) ) more than double the  Foreground Dice  ( \(0.4120\) )? 
 If this student changes post-processing thresholds and observes that  Foreground Dice  rises to  \(0.5200\) , but  Empty-Pair Accuracy  drops to  \(0.8100\) , what is the new  Competition Proxy Score ? 
 Did the threshold change represent a genuine overall improvement according to the competition objective? 
 
 
 8. Authoritative References 
 
 Dice, L. R. (1945).  Measures of the Amount of Ecologic Association Between Species . Ecology, 26(3), 297–302. 
 Sørensen, T. (1948).  A method of establishing groups of equal amplitude in plant sociology . Kongelige Danske Videnskabernes Selskab. 
 Taha, A. A., & Hanbury, A. (2015).  Metrics for evaluating 3D medical image segmentation: analysis, selection, and tool . BMC Medical Imaging. (Comprehensive review of overlap metrics, empty set conventions, and precision-recall trade-offs).

title: Guide 06 · Validation Error Analysis
text:
Validation Error Analysis and Spatial Defect Diagnostics 
 A single scalar metric—whether it is a validation loss of  \(0.18\)  or a Foreground Dice of  \(0.56\) —is a summary statistic. It tells you  how much  your model succeeded on average, but it tells you  nothing about why or how it failed . 
 Did your model achieve a low score because it completely missed hairline scratches? Because it hallucinated spurious defect blobs on clean steel strips? Because it confused surface inclusions ( defect_c ) with micro-cracks ( defect_b )? Or because it correctly located every defect but dilated boundaries by 10 pixels? 
 Each of these failure modes points toward a completely different engineering remedy. Tuning loss weights will not fix an encoder that downsampled thin cracks out of existence, and increasing training epochs will not eliminate speckle noise that requires connected-component filtering. 
 This guide establishes a disciplined, repeatable methodology for  visual and quantitative validation error analysis , categorizes the  six spatial error archetypes , introduces  defect size binning , and teaches students how to formulate testable diagnostic hypotheses. 
 
 1. Observable Problem: The Ambiguity of Aggregate Scores 
 Consider two models trained on the same validation fold, both reporting an identical aggregate metric: 
 Validation Summary Comparison:
Model Alpha:  Val Foreground Dice = 0.520
Model Beta:   Val Foreground Dice = 0.520

Looking deeper into the error decomposition:
Model Alpha Error Profile:
• Complete Defect Miss Rate: 48% (Misses almost half of all defects completely!)
• When Defect is Detected: Boundary Dice = 0.88 (Sub-pixel boundary precision!)
• Clean Strip False Alarms: 0.8% (Almost never hallucinates on clean material)
Diagnosis: High precision, severe recall failure. Model is overly conservative.

Model Beta Error Profile:
• Complete Defect Miss Rate: 4% (Detects 96% of all defects!)
• When Defect is Detected: Boundary Dice = 0.54 (Bloated, noisy, poorly localized borders)
• Clean Strip False Alarms: 32.4% (Floods clean material with spurious speckles)
Diagnosis: High recall, abysmal precision. Model is trigger-happy and noisy. 
 Treating Model Alpha and Model Beta identically because their aggregate Dice score is  \(0.520\)  would be a critical mistake. Model Alpha needs threshold lowering and rare-class loss weighting; Model Beta needs minimum area filtering and stronger background regularization. 
 
 2. The 4-View Visual Audit Workflow 
 To diagnose a model's spatial behavior, you must inspect validation predictions across four aligned visual channels simultaneously: 
 View 1: Raw Grayscale Strip (128 x 800)
• The unaugmented input image.
• Check: Is the defect visible to the human eye? Are there surface artifacts or lighting gradients?

View 2: Ground-Truth Mask (Binary 0 or 1)
• The annotated reference label for the target defect channel.
• Check: What is the defect geometry (thin scratch, clustered inclusion, diffuse patch)?

View 3: Continuous Probability Heatmap (P in [0, 1])
• The raw output of torch.sigmoid(logits) or softmax probabilities.
• Check: Is the model confident (P > 0.9), uncertain (P ≈ 0.4), or completely blind (P < 0.05)?
• Crucial: Distinguishes thresholding failures from representation failures.

View 4: Post-Processed Binary Mask (P >= tau and Area >= A_min)
• The final binary mask after thresholding and connected-component area filtering.
• Check: Does this prediction match the ground truth in Quadrant 1 overlap? 
 
 3. The Six Spatial Error Archetypes 
 
 Figure 6.1: Visual gallery of the six spatial error archetypes on synthetic line-scan strips ( \(128 \times 800\) ), showing the raw image, ground truth, continuous heatmap, and thresholded prediction. 
 Archetype A: The Completely Missed Defect (False Negative) 
 
 Visual Appearance : Ground truth shows a clear, thin longitudinal scratch; probability heatmap is completely dark ( \(P < 0.10\)  everywhere); binary prediction is blank. 
 Quantitative Signature : Ground-truth positive ( \(|Y| > 0\) ), Prediction area zero ( \(|P| = 0\) ),  \(\text{Dice} = 0.0\) . 
 Plausible Hypotheses : 
 Downsampling Elimination : If the encoder downsampled the image by  \(16\times\)  ( \(128 \to 8\) ,  \(800 \to 50\) ) and skip connections are broken or missing, a 2-pixel wide scratch vanished from the feature maps. 
 Class Starvation : If the defect is rare  defect_b , the optimizer received virtually zero gradient updates for this class. 
 Excessive Area Filtering : The model predicted the scratch, but connected-component post-processing discarded it because its total pixel area was below  \(A_{\min}\) . 
 
 
 
 Archetype B: False Alarm on Clean Material (Spurious Artifact) 
 
 Visual Appearance : Ground truth is completely blank; raw strip shows benign roller marks, oil droplets, or illumination falloff; probability heatmap shows high confidence ( \(P > 0.75\) ). 
 Quantitative Signature : Ground-truth empty ( \(|Y| = 0\) ), Prediction area positive ( \(|P| > 0\) ), Specificity penalty. 
 Plausible Hypotheses : 
 Oversampling Prior Shift : Training set was oversampled too aggressively with rare defect strips, teaching the model that defects are ubiquitous. 
 Deficient Training Augmentation : The model memorized specific camera lighting gradients because contrast jitter or CLAHE was omitted. 
 Threshold Too Permissive : Decision threshold  \(\tau\)  set too low (e.g.  \(\tau = 0.20\) ). 
 
 
 
 Archetype C: Channel / Class Confusion 
 
 Visual Appearance : A physical scratch is clearly present; the model outputs a confident prediction, but on the  wrong defect channel  (e.g., predicted on  defect_c  instead of  defect_a ). 
 Quantitative Signature : On channel A: False Negative ( \(\text{Dice} = 0\) ). On channel C: False Positive ( \(\text{Dice} = 0\) ). 
 Plausible Hypotheses : 
 Channel Conflict in Sigmoid Head : Independent sigmoid channels allow multiple classes to claim the same pixel; abundant class C dominates rare class A. 
 Feature Ambiguity : The receptive field of the network is too narrow to distinguish between an isolated inclusion and a short longitudinal scratch. 
 
 
 
 Archetype D: Salt-and-Pepper Speckle Noise 
 
 Visual Appearance : Scattered across the strip are dozens of tiny 1-to-5 pixel isolated activation islands. 
 Quantitative Signature : Prediction area is non-trivial ( \(|P| = 150\text{ px}\) ), but intersection with ground truth is near zero. 
 Plausible Hypotheses : 
 High-Frequency Sensor Noise Sensitivity : The model's stem convolutions are reacting to high-frequency image grain. 
 Absence of Connected-Component Filtering : Post-processing pipeline lacks minimum area filtering ( \(A_{\min} = 0\) ). 
 
 
 
 Archetype E: Boundary Dilation / Erosion / Misplacement 
 
 Visual Appearance : The model successfully identifies the defect location, but the predicted mask is bloated ( \(2\times\)  wider than ground truth) or shifted by several pixels. 
 Quantitative Signature : True positive overlap exists ( \(|P \cap Y| > 0\) ), but Dice is mediocre ( \(0.40\)  to  \(0.60\) ). 
 Plausible Hypotheses : 
 Receptive Field / Decoder Blur : Bilinear upsampling without fine skip-connection refinement causes blurry, diffuse activation borders. 
 Decision Threshold Misalignment : Threshold  \(\tau = 0.50\)  is cutting the probability sigmoid at the wrong slope point. 
 Loss Function Imbalance : Excessive  pos_weight  in BCE penalizes false negatives so heavily that the model expands borders outward to avoid missing edge pixels. 
 
 
 
 Archetype F: Fragmented or Bridged Defect Components 
 
 Visual Appearance : A continuous 300-pixel longitudinal crack is predicted as 5 disjoint islands with small 2-pixel gaps between them. 
 Quantitative Signature : Component count in prediction is high ( \(N_{\text{components}} = 5\) ) while ground truth has  \(N_{\text{components}} = 1\) . 
 Plausible Hypotheses : 
 Lack of Longitudinal Context : Convolutions lack wide horizontal receptive fields (dilated convolutions or horizontal pooling) to bridge gaps along the rolling direction ( \(800\text{ px}\) ). 
 
 
 
 
 4. Quantitative Diagnostics: Beyond Aggregate Dice 
 To make error analysis systematic across thousands of validation images, compute these four structural metrics: 
 Metric 1: Presence Detection Recall
• Formula: P(|P| > 0 | |Y| > 0)
• Measures: Did the model flag ANY pixels when a defect existed?
• Isolates: Pure detection sensitivity, independent of boundary shape.

Metric 2: Overlap Detection Recall
• Formula: P(|P ∩ Y| > 0 | |Y| > 0)
• Measures: Did the model actually intersect the true defect?
• Isolates: Distinguishes touching the defect from predicting somewhere else on the strip!

Metric 3: Conditional Overlap Dice
• Formula: Mean Dice evaluated ONLY on pairs where |P ∩ Y| > 0.
• Measures: When the model touches the defect, how well does it trace its borders?
• Isolates: Boundary segmentation quality from presence detection capability.

Metric 4: Defect Size Binning
• Group ground-truth defects into area tiers:
  - Small:    1 to 100 pixels
  - Medium: 101 to 500 pixels
  - Large:   > 500 pixels
• Measures: Overlap recall and Dice independently per size tier. 
 The Power of Defect Size Binning: 
 If your model achieves  \(0.88\)  Dice on large defects ( \(>500\text{ px}\) ),  \(0.65\)  Dice on medium defects, and  \(0.00\)  Dice on small defects ( \(1..100\text{ px}\) ) , you have isolated the exact architectural flaw:  downsampling loss in early encoder layers . You do not need to change your optimizer or loss weights; you need high-resolution skip connections or higher-resolution feature maps! 
 
 5. Fair Sampling: The "Cherry-Picking Trap" 
 When conducting visual error reviews, students naturally tend to sort errors by lowest Dice and inspect the 10 worst images. 
 
 [!WARNING]
 The Cherry-Picking Trap :
Reviewing only the "top-10 worst" images distorts your engineering priorities. The worst images are often annotation anomalies, ambiguous borderline samples, or extreme outliers. If you redesign your pipeline based on 5 extreme outliers, you may degrade performance across the remaining 2,000 normal validation images. 
 
 The Disciplined Stratified Audit Protocol: 
 Instead of inspecting only the worst cases, sample  30 validation images  according to an explicit stratified grid: 
 The 30-Image Stratified Audit Grid:
• 6 Clean Material Strips: Sampled at random from true-negative images.
  -> Check: Is the model staying completely silent? Are roller marks causing false alarms?
• 6 High-Performing Strips (Dice > 0.75):
  -> Check: What defect textures does the model handle effortlessly?
• 6 Boundary-Error Strips (Overlap hit, but Dice between 0.30 and 0.60):
  -> Check: Are boundaries dilated, eroded, or shifted?
• 6 Complete Misses (GT positive, Pred area = 0):
  -> Check: What size and class are the missed defects? Faint hairline cracks?
• 6 Rare Class Strips (Defect B):
  -> Check: Are rare defects detected, confused with other classes, or ignored? 
 
 6. Diagnostic Symptoms to Experimental Hypotheses 
 
 
 
 Error Pattern Observed in Audit 
 Plausible Root Causes 
 Distinguishing Observation 
 Formulated Testable Hypothesis 
 
 
 
 
 Small defects ( \(<100\text{ px}\) ) have  \(0\%\)  recall, while large defects have  \(85\%\)  recall. 
 A. Encoder downsamples too aggressively. B. Post-processing area filter ( \(A_{\min}\) ) is discarding small defects. 
 Inspect raw probability heatmap before area filtering. If  \(P > 0.5\)  exists before filtering, cause is B; if heatmap is dark, cause is A. 
 "Lowering  \(A_{\min}\)  for class A from 100 to 30 will increase small defect recall without sacrificing clean specificity." 
 
 
 Defect presence is detected ( \(P > 0.7\) ), but predicted mask is  \(3\times\)  thicker than ground truth. 
 A.  pos_weight  in BCE is too high. B. Decision threshold  \(\tau\)  is too low. C. Blur from decoder upsampling. 
 Inspect sigmoid probability contour lines. If probabilities taper gradually over 15 pixels, cause is C; if sharp but thresholded at 0.2, cause is B. 
 "Increasing decision threshold  \(\tau\)  from 0.35 to 0.55 will trim dilated boundaries and increase overlap Dice." 
 
 
 Continuous longitudinal scratches appear fragmented into 4 disjoint islands. 
 Convolutions lack sufficient horizontal receptive field along the 800-pixel rolling axis. 
 Measure gap distance between islands. Gaps are typically 2–5 pixels of slightly lower contrast. 
 "Adding horizontal dilation or applying morphological closing with a  \(1 \times 5\)  horizontal kernel will bridge fragmented components." 
 
 
 Model predicts  defect_c  at the exact location of a ground-truth  defect_a  scratch. 
 Channel confusion in multi-label head; class C has higher training prior than class A. 
 Compare raw logits of channel A vs channel C on the defect pixels. 
 "Switching from independent sigmoid channels to a mutually exclusive 5-way softmax head will force channels to compete explicitly." 
 
 
 
 
 7. Ungraded "Try It": Error Analysis Case Study 
 Review this audit log of 4 validation images from a student's pipeline: 
 Image STRIP_0104 (Clean Material):
• Ground Truth: All channels empty (0 px)
• Model Output: Channel C predicts 3 small blobs (12 px, 8 px, 18 px)
• Probability in Blobs: P ≈ 0.62

Image STRIP_0412 (Defect A Scratch):
• Ground Truth: Defect A scratch of 140 pixels (Height 2 px, Width 70 px)
• Model Output: Channel A predicts 0 pixels
• Continuous Heatmap: Peak probability along scratch is P = 0.38

Image STRIP_0821 (Defect D Patch):
• Ground Truth: Defect D patch of 650 pixels
• Model Output: Channel D predicts 1,420 pixels (Dice = 0.52)
• Continuous Heatmap: Bloated probability halo around true boundary

Image STRIP_1105 (Defect B Micro-crack):
• Ground Truth: Defect B crack of 85 pixels
• Model Output: Channel B predicts 0 pixels; Channel C predicts 80 pixels
• Continuous Heatmap: Channel C probability is P = 0.82; Channel B is P = 0.04 
 Diagnostic Questions : 
 
 For  STRIP_0104 , what post-processing technique would eliminate the 3 tiny false alarm blobs without changing model weights? 
 For  STRIP_0412 , why was the scratch missed if the heatmap showed  \(P = 0.38\) ? What would happen if threshold  \(\tau\)  was lowered to  \(0.35\) ? 
 For  STRIP_1105 , what error archetype occurred, and why did the model favor Channel C over Channel B? 
 
 
 8. Authoritative References 
 
 Hoiem, D., Chodpathumwan, Y., & Dai, Q. (2012).  Diagnosing Error in Object Detectors . European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV). (Foundational framework for categorized spatial error analysis). 
 OpenCV  Connected Components with Stats ( cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats ) . 
 Ronneberger, O., et al. (2015).  U-Net: Convolutional Networks for Biomedical Image Segmentation . MICCAI. (Receptive fields and skip connection mechanics).

title: Guide 07 · Controlled Experimentation
text:
Controlled Experimentation and Scientific Iteration 
 When training deep segmentation models, the temptation to try multiple promising ideas at once is overwhelming. A team might simultaneously swap their encoder backbone, add cosine learning-rate decay, introduce rare-class oversampling, switch from BCE to Focal Loss, and apply aggressive new augmentations—all in a single training run. 
 If the validation score drops, which change was responsible? More dangerously,  if the validation score improves by +0.03, did all five changes help—or did one brilliant change help by +0.07 while two harmful changes degraded performance by -0.04? 
 Without controlled experimentation, deep learning degenerates into superstitious trial-and-error. You waste hundreds of GPU hours chasing phantom improvements and deploying bloated pipelines with harmful components. 
 This final guide establishes the  scientific method for machine learning engineering : the One-Factor-At-A-Time (OFAT) protocol, invariant baselines, ablation methodology, and an experiment audit matrix to ensure every line of code in your pipeline is justified by rigorous empirical evidence. 
 
 1. Observable Problem: The Multi-Change Confusion 
 Consider this real-world interaction between two project logs: 
 Run 01: Baseline
Architecture: ResNet-34 U-Net | Loss: BCE + Soft Dice | Schedule: Constant 1e-3 | Sampling: Natural
Val Foreground Dice: 0.502 | Clean Specificity: 98.4%

Run 02: "The Kitchen Sink"
Student changes:
1. Switched encoder to EfficientNet-B2
2. Added Cosine Annealing with Warmup
3. Enabled 5x Rare-Class Oversampling
4. Replaced BCE with Focal Loss
5. Added Random Gamma & Contrast Augmentation
Val Foreground Dice: 0.518 (+0.016 improvement!) 
 The student declares Run 02 an unambiguous success and permanently adopts all five changes. 
 Two weeks later, the team conducts a systematic ablation study and discovers: 
 
 The  Cosine Annealing  schedule had actually improved the score by  +0.045 . 
 The  Focal Loss  and  5x Oversampling  had degraded performance by  -0.029  by flooding clean images with false alarms! 
 By bundling all changes together, the student had masked a severe degradation and locked two harmful components into their pipeline. 
 
 
 2. The Four Principles of Controlled Experimentation 
 
 Figure 7.1: The scientific iteration cycle in deep learning. Every experiment isolates a single factor, tests an explicit falsifiable hypothesis against a frozen baseline anchor, and reaches a definitive audit decision. 
 To achieve scientific attribution, adhere strictly to these four rules: 
 Principle 1: The One-Factor-At-A-Time (OFAT) Rule 
 In any individual experiment run,  change exactly one independent variable  relative to your established baseline anchor: 
 
 Change the learning-rate schedule, OR 
 Change the loss formulation, OR 
 Change the sampling rule, OR 
 Change the encoder architecture.
 Never change two simultaneously.  If an experiment changes both the optimizer and the dataset sampling, you cannot attribute the resulting score to either factor. 
 
 Principle 2: Freeze Invariant Foundations 
 Every experiment in a series must share an identical foundation: 
 
 Identical Validation Split : Always evaluate against the exact same combination-stratified fold (e.g. Fold 0). Never compare a Fold 0 score to a Fold 1 score or a random split. 
 Identical Preprocessing & Dimensions : Grayscale loading, standard normalization, and native  \(128 \times 800\)  resolution must remain fixed. 
 Identical Evaluation Protocol : The metric computation code, threshold evaluation grid, and minimum area filters must be identical. 
 Identical Random Seed : Keep data splitting, worker initialization, and augmentations seeded deterministically. 
 
 Principle 3: Formulate a Falsifiable Hypothesis 
 Before launching an experiment, write down an explicit hypothesis stating  why  the change should help and  what specific measurement  will confirm or refute it: 
 
 Poor Hypothesis : "I want to try cosine decay to see if it improves things." 
 Rigorous Scientific Hypothesis : "Because our baseline oscillates in narrow minima during the final 10 epochs, switching from constant LR to Cosine Annealing with a 3-epoch warmup will reduce late-stage loss variance and increase validation Foreground Dice on thin defects by at least  \(+0.02\) ." 
 
 Principle 4: Distinguish Signal from Stochastic Noise 
 Every deep learning run contains random variance from mini-batch shuffling and weight initialization. 
 
 If an experiment alters a hyperparameter and the validation Dice shifts from  \(0.562\)  to  \(0.564\)  ( \(+0.002\) ), this difference is within typical run-to-run noise! Do not declare victory. 
 A genuine architectural or algorithmic improvement typically produces a noticeable shift ( \(+0.015\)  to  \(+0.04\) ) or a marked change in error distributions. 
 When in doubt, repeat the run across two random seeds to verify that the gain is reproducible. 
 
 
 3. The Experiment Audit Matrix 
 Maintain a structured experiment tracking matrix (in Weights & Biases or a markdown table) that records every run:

 Notice how every single improvement was isolated, attributed, and validated independently. 
 
 4. The Anatomy of an Ablation Study 
 An  ablation study  is the inverse of iterative optimization: you take your best high-performing pipeline and systematically  remove or disable one component at a time  to verify that each component is strictly necessary. 
 Full Optimized Pipeline:
[EfficientNet-B2] + [Warmup+Cosine] + [Bounded Rare Sampling] + [Calibrated Area Filter]
Score: 0.589

Ablation 1: Remove Bounded Rare Sampling (revert to Natural Uniform)
Score drops to 0.552 (-0.037) -> Proves that rare sampling is vital for Defect B recall.

Ablation 2: Remove Cosine Schedule (revert to Constant LR)
Score drops to 0.544 (-0.045) -> Proves that schedule decay is vital for boundary annealing.

Ablation 3: Remove Area Filtering (revert to A_min = 0 for all classes)
Score drops to 0.574 (-0.015) -> Proves that speckle suppression provides a real precision boost. 
 If removing a component causes  zero drop in score , that component is dead weight! Delete it from your codebase immediately to keep your system lean, fast, and maintainable. 
 
 5. Common Experimentation Anti-Patterns 
 
 The "Kaggle Leaderboard Overfitting" Anti-Pattern : 
 Submitting every single training run to the public leaderboard and using the public score to guide hyperparameter decisions. 
 Why it fails : The public leaderboard represents a small subset of the test set. Over-tuning to it causes public overfitting, leading to massive leaderboard shakeup on the private test set. Trust your local combination-stratified validation fold! 
 
 
 The "Comparing Uncalibrated Models" Anti-Pattern : 
 Comparing Model X at threshold  \(\tau = 0.50\)  against Model Y at threshold  \(\tau = 0.50\) , when Model X's optimal threshold is  \(0.35\)  and Model Y's optimal threshold is  \(0.65\) . 
 Why it fails : Always calibrate decision thresholds and area filters on held-out validation data before declaring one architecture superior to another. 
 
 
 The "Changing Seeds to Find a Lucky Run" Anti-Pattern : 
 Re-running the identical model with seeds 41, 42, 43, 44, and 45 until one seed achieves a slightly higher score, then claiming an improvement. 
 Why it fails : This is statistical noise, not architectural progress. 
 
 
 
 
 6. Ungraded "Try It": Design an Experiment Plan 
 Imagine you have just established a baseline model with the following characteristics: 
 
 Validation Foreground Dice:  \(0.48\) 
 Clean Material Specificity:  \(98.8\%\) 
 Rare Defect B Recall:  \(0.0\%\)  (Completely missed) 
 Small Defect ( \(<100\text{ px}\) ) Recall:  \(12\%\) 
 
 You have a research budget of  4 experiments . 
 Task : Formulate a sequential 4-step experimental plan: 
 
 What single factor will you test in Experiment 1? State your hypothesis. 
 If Experiment 1 succeeds, what factor will you test in Experiment 2? 
 What negative symptom will you monitor in your experiment logs to ensure that clean-material performance is not sacrificed? 
 
 
 7. Authoritative References 
 
 Sculley, D., et al. (2015).  Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems . Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS). (Foundational reference on pipeline complexity, dead code, and ablation discipline). 
 Bouthillier, X., et al. (2021).  Accounting for variance in machine learning benchmarks . Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems (MLSys). (Empirical variance and seed significance). 
 Weights & Biases  Experiment Tracking Best Practices .

title: Walkthrough Notebook & Code Examples
text:
Milestone 4: Synthetic Optimization Walkthrough Notebook 
 This folder contains a standalone, CPU-runnable pedagogical walkthrough of training improvements and model optimization techniques: 
 
 Jupyter Notebook :  synthetic_optimization_walkthrough.ipynb 
 Paired Python Script :  synthetic_optimization_walkthrough.py 
 
 
 What This Walkthrough Demonstrates 
 
 Multi-Level Class Imbalance & Bounded Sampling : 
 Synthesizes an imbalanced dataset containing clean strips (~50%), frequent defects ( defect_c ), and rare defects ( defect_b ). 
 Implements a bounded sqrt inverse-frequency  WeightedRandomSampler  to boost rare-defect exposure without starving clean material. 
 
 
 Learning Rate Schedulers (Linear Warmup + Cosine Decay) : 
 Configures  torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR  to execute a 3-epoch linear warmup followed by smooth cosine decay down to 1% of initial learning rate ( min_lr_ratio = 0.01 ). 
 
 
 Early Stopping & Checkpoint Rollback : 
 Implements an  EarlyStoppingTracker  with  mode='max' ,  min_delta , and  patience . 
 Simulates validation metric jitter, triggers early stopping, and restores best checkpoint weights. 
 
 
 PyTorch 2.x Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) & Gradient Accumulation : 
 Simulates  torch.amp.autocast  and  torch.amp.GradScaler  on toy tensors. 
 Demonstrates microbatch accumulation, unscaling, gradient norm clipping ( clip_grad_norm_ ), and optimizer stepping. 
 
 
 Metric Governance & The "Naive Dice Trap" : 
 Decomposes segmentation metrics into naive mean Dice, foreground-pair Dice, and clean-image specificity. 
 Proves mathematically why predicting all zeros achieves a deceptive >90% naive Dice while scoring 0.00 on actual defects. 
 
 
 Spatial Error Auditing : 
 Stratifies defect recall across area bins (small 1..100 px, medium 101..500 px, large >500 px). 
 Separates presence recall from spatial overlap hit. 
 
 
 
 
 How to Run 
 Option A: Local Terminal Execution with  uv 
 Run the paired Python script directly from your terminal:
 uv run python docs/milestone_4_student_guide/notebooks/synthetic_optimization_walkthrough.py 
Execution finishes in under 3 seconds on CPU. 
 Option B: Jupyter Lab / Notebook 
 Launch your local Jupyter server:
 uv run jupyter lab docs/milestone_4_student_guide/notebooks/synthetic_optimization_walkthrough.ipynb 
 Option C: Google Colab 
 
 Upload  synthetic_optimization_walkthrough.ipynb  to Google Colab. 
 Select a CPU runtime (no GPU is required for this synthetic demonstration). 
 Run the cells in sequential order. 
 
 
 Pedagogical Boundaries & Guarantees 
 
 100% Synthetic Data : This notebook generates all images and annotations procedurally. 
 Zero Competition Leaks : No raw images, real test IDs, private EDA numbers, or competition results are included. 
 Hardware Agnostic : Fully tested on standard CPU environments using PyTorch 2.8.0.
